note: The Atlas curriculum, with study notes for every topic. Topic titles and notes are English (British spelling), like the anatomy content. A topic lists `modules` where an available module teaches its core structures.

topics.title: Pectoral Region
topics.summary: The front of the upper chest wall, over the thorax. It holds the breast and the pectoral muscles that link the upper limb to the trunk.
points: Pectoralis major has clavicular and sternocostal heads; it adducts and medially rotates the arm and is supplied by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves.
Pectoralis minor runs from ribs 3 to 5 to the coracoid process of the scapula and divides the axillary artery into three parts.
The breast lies on the deep fascia over pectoralis major; its suspensory (Cooper’s) ligaments explain the skin dimpling over some breast cancers.
About 75% of the lymph from the breast drains to the axillary nodes, most of the rest to the parasternal nodes.

topics.title: Axilla
topics.summary: The pyramid-shaped space between the upper limb and the side of the chest: the passage for the vessels and nerves of the arm.
points: Its apex, the cervico-axillary canal between the clavicle, first rib and scapula, opens into the root of the neck.
Walls: anterior, pectoralis major and minor; posterior, subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi; medial, serratus anterior; lateral, the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
It contains the axillary artery and vein, the cords and branches of the brachial plexus, and lymph nodes embedded in fat.
Axillary lymph nodes are grouped as pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), humeral (lateral), central and apical.

topics.title: Scapular Region
topics.summary: The back of the shoulder around the scapula, with the muscles that move the scapula and steady the shoulder joint.
points: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor arise from the back of the scapula and subscapularis from its front; together they form the rotator cuff.
The suprascapular nerve passes below the superior transverse scapular ligament and the suprascapular artery above it.
The quadrangular space (teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps and the humerus) transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery.
The scapular anastomosis links branches of the subclavian and axillary arteries and can keep the limb supplied if the artery is blocked between them.

topics.title: Arm
topics.summary: The region between the shoulder and the elbow, built around the humerus, with an anterior (flexor) and a posterior (extensor) compartment.
points: Anterior compartment: biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis, all supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.
Posterior compartment: triceps brachii, supplied by the radial nerve.
The brachial artery continues the axillary artery at the lower border of teres major and divides into the radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa.
The radial nerve runs in the radial groove on the back of the humerus, where a fracture of the shaft can injure it and cause wrist drop.

topics.title: Cubital Fossa
topics.summary: The triangular hollow at the front of the elbow, through which the main vessels and nerves pass into the forearm.
points: Boundaries: a line joining the humeral epicondyles above, pronator teres medially and brachioradialis laterally.
Main contents from lateral to medial: the biceps tendon, the brachial artery and the median nerve (“TAN”); the radial nerve lies deep under brachioradialis.
The bicipital aponeurosis protects the artery and nerve; the median cubital vein runs superficial to it, which makes the fossa a common site for venepuncture.
The brachial artery usually divides into the radial and ulnar arteries here, at about the level of the neck of the radius.

topics.title: Forearm
topics.summary: The region between the elbow and the wrist. The radius and ulna are joined by the interosseous membrane, between an anterior flexor-pronator and a posterior extensor-supinator compartment.
points: Anterior compartment muscles are supplied by the median nerve, except flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, which the ulnar nerve supplies.
Posterior compartment muscles are supplied by the radial nerve, mostly through its deep branch (the posterior interosseous nerve).
Pronation and supination take place at the proximal and distal radio-ulnar joints as the radius turns around the ulna.
Raised pressure inside a closed compartment (compartment syndrome) threatens muscles and nerves and needs urgent fasciotomy.

topics.title: Wrist and Hand
topics.summary: Eight carpal bones, five metacarpals and fourteen phalanges, moved by long tendons from the forearm and by the small (intrinsic) muscles of the hand.
points: The carpal bones lie in two rows; the scaphoid is the one most often fractured, typically in a fall on the outstretched hand.
The carpal tunnel, roofed by the flexor retinaculum, carries the median nerve and nine flexor tendons; compression of the nerve causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the flexor retinaculum, through Guyon’s canal.
Most intrinsic muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve; the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles (through its recurrent branch) and the first two lumbricals.

topics.title: Gluteal Region
topics.summary: The buttock, behind the pelvis, from the iliac crest down to the gluteal fold.
points: Gluteus maximus (inferior gluteal nerve) extends the hip; gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve) abduct it and keep the pelvis level when walking.
If gluteus medius and minimus are weak, the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on one leg: a positive Trendelenburg sign.
The sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, usually below piriformis; the superior gluteal vessels and nerve pass above it.
Intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant or at the ventrogluteal site to keep away from the sciatic nerve.

topics.title: Thigh
topics.summary: The region between the hip and the knee, divided by intermuscular septa into anterior, medial and posterior compartments.
points: Anterior compartment: quadriceps femoris and sartorius, supplied by the femoral nerve.
Medial compartment: the adductors and gracilis, supplied mainly by the obturator nerve.
Posterior compartment: the hamstrings, supplied by the sciatic nerve.

The femoral triangle (inguinal ligament, sartorius and adductor longus) holds, from lateral to medial, the femoral nerve, artery and vein; the adductor canal then carries the vessels down to the popliteal fossa.

topics.title: Popliteal Fossa
topics.summary: The diamond-shaped space behind the knee, through which the vessels and nerves pass from the thigh into the leg.
points: Boundaries: biceps femoris above and laterally, semimembranosus and semitendinosus above and medially, and the two heads of gastrocnemius below.
From superficial to deep: the tibial nerve, the popliteal vein and the popliteal artery, which lies on the femur and the knee capsule.
The common fibular nerve follows the biceps tendon laterally and winds round the neck of the fibula.
A popliteal (Baker’s) cyst is a swelling of the bursa between semimembranosus and the medial head of gastrocnemius.

topics.title: Leg
topics.summary: The region between the knee and the ankle, around the tibia and fibula, with anterior, lateral and posterior compartments.
points: Anterior compartment: tibialis anterior and the long toe extensors, supplied by the deep fibular nerve; they dorsiflex the foot.
Lateral compartment: fibularis longus and brevis, supplied by the superficial fibular nerve; they evert the foot.
Posterior compartment: gastrocnemius, soleus and the deep flexors, supplied by the tibial nerve; they plantarflex and invert the foot.
The anterior compartment is a common site of compartment syndrome, for example after a fracture of the tibia.

topics.title: Ankle and Foot
topics.summary: The ankle joint and the bones, joints, ligaments and arches of the foot, built to bear weight and to act as a lever in walking.
points: The ankle (talocrural) joint is a hinge between the tibia, the fibula and the talus, allowing dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.
Inversion and eversion take place mainly at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints.
Inversion sprains tear the lateral ligament, most often the anterior talofibular part; the strong medial (deltoid) ligament resists eversion.
The arches are held up by the shape of the bones, the spring and plantar ligaments, the plantar aponeurosis and the muscles of the leg and foot.

topics.title: Thoracic Wall
topics.summary: The bony and muscular cage that protects the heart and lungs and moves in breathing.
points: It is formed by the twelve thoracic vertebrae, twelve pairs of ribs with their costal cartilages, and the sternum (manubrium, body and xiphoid process).
Each intercostal space holds external, internal and innermost intercostal muscles; the vein, artery and nerve run in that order from above in the groove under each rib.
The sternal angle marks the second costal cartilage, the T4/T5 level, the bifurcation of the trachea and the beginning and end of the aortic arch.
Chest drains and needles are passed just above a rib so they miss the neurovascular bundle under the rib above.

topics.title: Mediastinum
topics.summary: The central compartment of the thorax, between the two pleural cavities, from the sternum to the vertebral column.
points: A plane through the sternal angle and the T4/T5 disc divides it into the superior mediastinum and the inferior mediastinum, which has anterior, middle and posterior parts.
Superior mediastinum: the thymus (or its remnant), the great vessels, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct and the phrenic and vagus nerves.
Middle mediastinum: the heart in its pericardium with the roots of the great vessels. Posterior mediastinum: the descending aorta, oesophagus, azygos veins and thoracic duct.
A widened mediastinum on a chest radiograph can be a sign of aortic injury or enlarged lymph nodes.

topics.title: Pleural Cavities
topics.summary: The two serous spaces that surround the lungs and let them glide against the chest wall as they expand.
points: Visceral pleura covers each lung and is continuous at the hilum with the parietal pleura, which lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum.
The pleural cavity is a potential space with a thin film of fluid; air in it (pneumothorax) or fluid (pleural effusion) lets the lung collapse.
The costodiaphragmatic recesses are not filled by lung in quiet breathing; fluid collects there first in an upright patient.
Surface marking: the pleura reaches rib 8 in the mid-clavicular line, rib 10 in the mid-axillary line and rib 12 at the back; the lower border of the lung lies about two ribs higher.

topics.title: Anterior Abdominal Wall
topics.summary: The layered muscular wall at the front of the abdomen, which protects the viscera and moves the trunk.
points: From outside in: skin, superficial fascia (fatty and membranous layers), external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat and parietal peritoneum.
Rectus abdominis lies in the rectus sheath; above the arcuate line the sheath encloses it front and back, below it every aponeurosis passes in front.
It is supplied by the anterior rami of T7 to T12 and L1 (iliohypogastric and ilio-inguinal nerves); T10 supplies the skin around the umbilicus.
The linea alba, the midline raphe, is relatively avascular, so midline incisions are made through it.

topics.title: Posterior Abdominal Wall
topics.summary: The back wall of the abdominal cavity, behind the peritoneum, on which the kidneys and great vessels lie.
points: It is formed by the lumbar vertebrae, psoas major, quadratus lumborum, iliacus and the crura of the diaphragm.
The lumbar plexus (L1 to L4) forms within psoas major; its branches include the femoral, obturator, genitofemoral and lateral cutaneous femoral nerves.
The abdominal aorta and the inferior vena cava lie on the vertebral bodies, the aorta to the left.
The kidneys, ureters and adrenal (suprarenal) glands lie against it, behind the peritoneum.

topics.title: Inguinal Region
topics.summary: The groin: the junction of the abdominal wall and the thigh, where the inguinal canal passes through the abdominal wall.
points: The inguinal canal is about 4 cm long and runs above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial ring.
It carries the spermatic cord in males and the round ligament of the uterus in females, together with the ilio-inguinal nerve.
An indirect inguinal hernia enters the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; a direct hernia pushes through the inguinal (Hesselbach’s) triangle, medial to them.
The deep ring lies just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament; the superficial ring lies above and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

topics.title: Peritoneal Cavity
topics.summary: The potential space between the parietal peritoneum lining the abdominal wall and the visceral peritoneum covering many abdominal organs.
points: It is closed in males; in females it opens to the exterior through the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina.
It is divided into the greater sac and the lesser sac (omental bursa), which connect through the omental (epiploic) foramen.
Mesenteries, omenta and peritoneal ligaments carry vessels and nerves to the intraperitoneal organs.
Visceral peritoneum has visceral nerves, so its pain is poorly localised; parietal peritoneum has somatic nerves, so its pain is sharp and well localised.

topics.title: Retroperitoneum
topics.summary: The space behind the parietal peritoneum of the posterior abdominal wall.
points: Primarily retroperitoneal organs developed there: the kidneys, ureters, adrenal glands, abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava.
Secondarily retroperitoneal organs were pressed against the wall during development: most of the duodenum, the pancreas except its tail, and the ascending and descending colon.
Retroperitoneal organs have peritoneum on their front surface only and are relatively fixed in position.
Bleeding into this space, as from a ruptured aortic aneurysm, can be large and hidden; flank bruising (Grey Turner’s sign) may appear later.

topics.title: Pelvic Cavity
topics.summary: The space within the lesser (true) pelvis, below the pelvic inlet, holding the bladder, rectum and internal reproductive organs.
points: It is bounded by the sacrum, coccyx and hip bones and closed below by the pelvic floor.
It contains the urinary bladder, the end of the ureters, the rectum and the internal reproductive organs.
The female pelvis has a wider, rounder inlet and a wider subpubic angle than the male, suited to childbirth.
The internal iliac arteries supply the pelvic walls and organs; the sacral plexus lies on piriformis on the posterior wall.

topics.title: Pelvic Floor
topics.summary: The muscular sheet that closes the bottom of the pelvic cavity and supports the pelvic organs.
points: It is formed mainly by the pelvic diaphragm: levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus) and coccygeus.
Puborectalis forms a sling round the anorectal junction that helps keep faecal continence.
It is supplied by the nerve to levator ani (from S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4).
Damage during childbirth can lead to stress urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse; pelvic floor exercises strengthen it.

topics.title: Ischioanal Fossa
topics.summary: A fat-filled, wedge-shaped space on each side of the anal canal, below the pelvic diaphragm.
points: Its medial wall is formed by levator ani and the external anal sphincter; its lateral wall by obturator internus and its fascia.
The pudendal (Alcock’s) canal in its lateral wall carries the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels.
The fat lets the anal canal widen during defecation.
The two fossae communicate behind the anal canal, so an abscess can spread from one side to the other (horseshoe abscess).

topics.title: Scalp and Face
topics.summary: The soft tissues covering the vault of the skull, and the face with its muscles of expression and rich sensory supply.
points: Layers of the scalp: Skin, dense Connective tissue, epicranial Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue and Pericranium (SCALP).
Scalp wounds bleed heavily because the dense connective tissue holds the vessels open; infection spreads in the loose areolar layer.
The muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve (VII); the skin of the face by the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve (V1, V2 and V3).
The facial vein connects with the cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins, so infection near the nose can spread inside the skull.

topics.title: Temporal and Infratemporal Fossae
topics.summary: Two connected spaces on the side of the skull: the temporal fossa above the zygomatic arch and the infratemporal fossa below it, deep to the ramus of the mandible.
points: The temporal fossa holds temporalis; the infratemporal fossa holds the lateral and medial pterygoid muscles.
The infratemporal fossa also contains the maxillary artery, the pterygoid venous plexus, the mandibular nerve (V3) and the chorda tympani.
All four muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis and the two pterygoids) are supplied by V3; the lateral pterygoid opens the jaw.
The middle meningeal artery branches from the maxillary artery here and enters the skull through the foramen spinosum.

topics.title: Pterygopalatine Fossa
topics.summary: A small, pyramid-shaped space behind the maxilla and below the apex of the orbit: a crossroads for nerves and vessels of the face.
points: It contains the maxillary nerve (V2), the pterygopalatine ganglion and the last part of the maxillary artery.

It opens into the orbit (inferior orbital fissure), the nasal cavity (sphenopalatine foramen), the middle cranial fossa (foramen rotundum), the mouth (palatine canals) and the infratemporal fossa (pterygomaxillary fissure).
The pterygopalatine ganglion is parasympathetic: fibres from the greater petrosal nerve relay there to supply the lacrimal gland and the glands of the nose and palate.
The sphenopalatine artery, a terminal branch of the maxillary artery, is a source of severe posterior nosebleeds.

topics.title: Orbit
topics.summary: The bony socket that holds and protects the eye, with its muscles, nerves, vessels and the lacrimal gland.
points: Seven bones form it: frontal, zygomatic, maxilla, ethmoid, lacrimal, sphenoid and palatine.
Six extraocular muscles move the eye (four recti and two obliques); levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelid.
The lateral rectus is supplied by VI, the superior oblique by IV and all the others by III (“LR6 SO4”).
The optic canal carries the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery; the superior orbital fissure carries III, IV, VI, branches of V1 and the superior ophthalmic vein.

topics.title: Nasal Cavity and Paranasal Sinuses
topics.summary: The airway behind the nose, which warms, moistens and filters air, and the air-filled spaces in the surrounding bones that drain into it.
points: The septum divides the cavity; each lateral wall has superior, middle and inferior conchae with a meatus beneath each.
There are four paired sinuses: frontal, maxillary, ethmoidal and sphenoidal, lined by respiratory mucosa.
The frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoidal sinuses drain into the middle meatus; the nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus.
Most nosebleeds come from Kiesselbach’s (Little’s) area on the front of the septum, where several arteries meet.

topics.title: Oral Cavity
topics.summary: The mouth, from the lips to the palatoglossal arches, with the teeth, tongue, palate and openings of the salivary glands.
points: It has a vestibule (between lips, cheeks and teeth) and the oral cavity proper (inside the dental arches).
The hard palate is formed by the maxillae and palatine bones; the soft palate rises in swallowing to close off the nasopharynx.
The tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII), except palatoglossus, supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus.
Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue runs in the chorda tympani (VII) and from the posterior third in IX; general sensation of the anterior two-thirds in the lingual nerve (V3).

topics.title: Pharynx
topics.summary: The muscular tube behind the nose, mouth and larynx, shared by the airway and the food passage, from the skull base to C6.
points: It has three parts: the nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx, and continues as the oesophagus at C6.
Its outer circular layer is formed by the superior, middle and inferior constrictors; its inner longitudinal layer by stylopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus.
Its muscles are supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus, except stylopharyngeus, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).
The pharyngeal (adenoid), tubal, palatine and lingual tonsils form a ring of lymphoid tissue (Waldeyer’s ring).

topics.title: Larynx
topics.summary: The voice box: a cartilage framework that guards the airway and produces the voice, from C3 to C6 in adults.
points: Its cartilages are the thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis (single) and the arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform (paired).
All its intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, except cricothyroid, supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that opens (abducts) the vocal folds.
In an emergency the airway can be opened through the cricothyroid membrane (cricothyroidotomy).

topics.title: Ear
topics.summary: The organ of hearing and balance, in three parts: external, middle and inner ear.
points: External ear: the auricle and the external acoustic meatus, ending at the tympanic membrane.
Middle ear: the malleus, incus and stapes carry vibrations to the oval window; the pharyngotympanic (auditory) tube balances the pressure.
Inner ear, in the petrous temporal bone: the cochlea for hearing and the vestibule and semicircular canals for balance, supplied by the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII).
Stapedius (supplied by VII) and tensor tympani (supplied by V3) damp the vibrations of loud sounds.

topics.title: Triangles of the Neck
topics.summary: Sternocleidomastoid divides each side of the neck into an anterior and a posterior triangle, a framework for finding structures in the neck.
points: The anterior triangle is subdivided into the submandibular, submental, carotid and muscular triangles.
The carotid triangle contains the carotid bifurcation, the internal jugular vein and the vagus and hypoglossal nerves.
The posterior triangle contains the accessory nerve (XI), which lies superficially and is easily injured, and in its lower part the trunks of the brachial plexus.
Lymph nodes in both triangles are examined in every head and neck assessment.

topics.title: Root of the Neck
topics.summary: The junction of the neck and the thorax, around the superior thoracic aperture.
points: The aperture is bounded by T1, the first pair of ribs and the manubrium.
It contains the subclavian vessels, the brachiocephalic veins, the vagus and phrenic nerves, the thoracic duct and the dome of the pleura.
Scalenus anterior is the key landmark: the phrenic nerve lies on it, the subclavian vein in front of it, and the subclavian artery and brachial plexus behind it.
The dome of the pleura rises above the medial end of the clavicle, so a needle placed here can cause a pneumothorax.

topics.title: Cranial Cavity
topics.summary: The inside of the skull, which holds the brain, its meninges and the dural venous sinuses.
points: The anterior cranial fossa holds the frontal lobes; the middle fossa the temporal lobes and pituitary gland; the posterior fossa the cerebellum and brainstem.
The dura forms the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli and encloses the dural venous sinuses.
Foramina carry the cranial nerves: for example, the foramen magnum transmits the medulla and vertebral arteries, and the jugular foramen IX, X, XI and the internal jugular vein.
Raised intracranial pressure can push brain tissue through the tentorial notch or the foramen magnum (herniation).

topics.title: Osteogenesis and Bone Remodelling
topics.summary: How bone forms during development and is continually broken down and rebuilt throughout life.
points: Intramembranous ossification turns mesenchyme directly into bone: the flat bones of the skull vault and most of the clavicle form this way.
Endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model with bone; long bones grow in length at their epiphyseal (growth) plates until early adulthood.
Osteoblasts lay down osteoid, which mineralises; osteoclasts resorb bone; osteocytes in their lacunae sense mechanical load.
Remodelling responds to load and to parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and calcitonin; when resorption outpaces formation, osteoporosis results.

topics.title: Syndesmology
topics.summary: The study of joints and ligaments (arthrology).
points: Joints are classified by their tissue as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial.
Ligaments are dense regular connective tissue that join bone to bone and limit movement.
A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint united by a ligament or membrane, such as the distal tibiofibular joint or the interosseous membrane of the forearm.
Ligament sprains are graded from stretching (grade I) through partial tear (grade II) to complete rupture (grade III).

topics.title: Kinesiology
topics.summary: The study of human movement, drawing on anatomy, biomechanics and physiology.
points: Flexion and extension take place in the sagittal plane, abduction and adduction in the coronal plane and rotation in the transverse plane.
Muscles act as prime movers (agonists), antagonists, synergists and fixators.
In a concentric contraction the muscle shortens; in an eccentric contraction it lengthens under load; in an isometric contraction its length does not change.
Most of the body’s levers are third-class (effort between the fulcrum and the load), favouring speed and range of movement over force.

topics.title: Haemodynamics
topics.summary: The physics of blood flow: pressure, flow and resistance in the circulation.
points: Flow equals the pressure difference divided by the resistance (Q = ΔP/R).
By Poiseuille’s law resistance varies with the inverse of the fourth power of the radius, so small changes in arteriolar diameter change flow greatly.
Mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance; cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate.
Flow is normally laminar; turbulence, for example at a narrowed valve or artery, produces murmurs and bruits.

topics.title: Microcirculation
topics.summary: The arterioles, capillaries and venules, where blood exchanges gases, nutrients and waste with the tissues.
points: Arterioles are the main site of resistance and control the flow into each capillary bed.
Capillaries are continuous (muscle, brain), fenestrated (renal glomeruli, intestine, endocrine glands) or sinusoidal (liver, spleen, bone marrow).
Hydrostatic and oncotic pressures (Starling forces) govern fluid movement across the capillary wall; lymphatics return the excess.
Oedema forms when filtration exceeds lymphatic drainage, as with raised venous pressure or low plasma protein.

topics.title: Lymphoid Organs
topics.summary: The organs in which lymphocytes develop and immune responses begin.
points: Primary lymphoid organs, where lymphocytes mature: the red bone marrow (B cells) and the thymus (T cells).
Secondary lymphoid organs, where responses start: the lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.
Lymph nodes filter lymph; B cells gather in follicles in the cortex and T cells in the paracortex.
The spleen filters blood: its red pulp removes old red cells and its white pulp mounts immune responses. After splenectomy the risk of infection by encapsulated bacteria rises.

topics.title: Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue
topics.summary: Unencapsulated lymphoid tissue in the lining of the gut, airways and urogenital tract, guarding the body’s largest surfaces (MALT).
points: It includes the tonsils, Peyer’s patches in the ileum and the lymphoid tissue of the appendix.
Microfold (M) cells over Peyer’s patches carry antigens from the gut lumen to the immune cells beneath.
Its plasma cells make IgA, which is secreted onto mucosal surfaces.
Chronic stimulation, as by Helicobacter pylori infection in the stomach, can lead to MALT lymphoma.

topics.title: Bronchopulmonary Segments
topics.summary: The functional units of the lung, each supplied by its own segmental bronchus and branch of the pulmonary artery.
points: The right lung has 10 segments; the left lung has 8 to 10, because some segments share a bronchus.
Segmental (tertiary) bronchi and arteries run in the centre of each segment; pulmonary veins run between segments.
Because each segment is self-contained, a diseased segment can be removed on its own (segmentectomy).
In a patient lying on their back, inhaled material often enters the superior segment of the right lower lobe.

topics.title: Hepatobiliary System
topics.summary: The liver, gallbladder and bile ducts, which make, store and deliver bile.
points: The liver receives about 75% of its blood from the hepatic portal vein and about 25% from the hepatic artery.
It is divided into eight functional (Couinaud) segments, each with its own portal triad and venous drainage, so segments can be removed separately.
Bile flows through the right and left hepatic ducts into the common hepatic duct, which joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct.
The common bile duct usually joins the main pancreatic duct and opens into the second part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.

topics.title: Gastrointestinal Tract
topics.summary: The continuous tube from mouth to anus that digests food and absorbs nutrients and water.
points: Its wall has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa (inner circular and outer longitudinal) and serosa or adventitia.
The foregut, midgut and hindgut are supplied by the coeliac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery and the inferior mesenteric artery.
The small intestine absorbs most nutrients; the large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes.
Pain from the foregut is felt in the epigastrium, from the midgut around the umbilicus and from the hindgut above the pubis.

topics.title: Enteric Nervous System
topics.summary: The gut’s own nervous system, in the wall of the digestive tract from the oesophagus to the anus.
points: It contains hundreds of millions of neurons and can run reflexes such as peristalsis without input from the brain.
The myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus, between the muscle layers, mainly controls movement; the submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus mainly controls secretion and local blood flow.
Sympathetic and parasympathetic (mainly vagal) nerves adjust its activity.
Absence of its ganglion cells in the distal colon causes Hirschsprung’s disease, with obstruction from birth.

topics.title: Nephrology Anatomy
topics.summary: The structure of the kidneys and urinary drainage, as the basis for renal medicine.
points: Each kidney has an outer cortex and an inner medulla of renal pyramids; urine drains through the minor and major calyces into the renal pelvis.
The nephron is made of the renal corpuscle (glomerulus and Bowman’s capsule), proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and collecting duct.
Segmental branches of the renal artery are end arteries, so blocking one causes infarction of that segment.
The kidneys lie at about T12 to L3, the right slightly lower than the left because of the liver.

topics.title: Neuroendocrinology
topics.summary: How the nervous system and the hormone system work together.
points: Hypothalamic neurons release releasing and inhibiting hormones into the hypophyseal portal veins to control the anterior pituitary.
Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) and oxytocin are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and released from the posterior pituitary.
The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion that releases adrenaline and noradrenaline into the blood.
Hormone levels are held steady mainly by negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary.

topics.title: Special Visceral Afferent Systems
topics.summary: In the classical classification of cranial nerve fibres, the special visceral afferents carry taste and smell.
points: Smell is carried by the olfactory nerve (I) to the olfactory bulb.
Taste is carried by the facial nerve (anterior two-thirds of the tongue), glossopharyngeal nerve (posterior third) and vagus nerve (epiglottis region).
All taste fibres end in the nucleus of the solitary tract in the brainstem.
Taste then relays in the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus to the insula and frontal operculum.

topics.title: General Somatic Afferent Systems
topics.summary: The fibres that carry pain, temperature, touch, pressure and proprioception from the skin, muscles and joints.
points: In the body they travel in the spinal nerves; in the head mainly in the trigeminal nerve.
Their cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglia or, for the face, in the trigeminal ganglion.
Fine touch, vibration and proprioception ascend in the dorsal columns; pain and temperature in the spinothalamic tracts.
Testing these modalities separately helps locate a lesion in the nervous system.

topics.title: Fascial Space Anatomy
topics.summary: The spaces bounded by layers of fascia, which guide the spread of infection, fluid, blood and tumour.
points: In the neck, the retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal and alar fasciae; behind it the “danger space” between the alar and prevertebral fasciae runs down into the posterior mediastinum.
Ludwig’s angina is a spreading infection of the submandibular space that can block the airway.
In the hand, the thenar and midpalmar spaces and the flexor tendon sheaths can trap pus.
The deep fascia that encloses each limb compartment explains how swelling inside it can cause compartment syndrome.

topics.title: Surgical Planes and Approaches
topics.summary: The routes surgeons take through the body, chosen to reach a target safely along natural tissue planes.
points: Bloodless planes between layers of embryonic origin are followed, for example behind the colon and its mesentery when the colon is mobilised.
Total mesorectal excision removes the rectum inside its intact fascial envelope and lowers the local recurrence of rectal cancer.
Internervous planes run between muscles supplied by different nerves, such as the deltopectoral approach to the shoulder, so that no muscle loses its nerve supply.
Where possible, incisions follow the skin tension (Langer’s) lines, which gives better scars.

topics.title: Transplant Anatomy
topics.summary: The vessels, ducts and spaces that matter when an organ is moved from a donor to a recipient.
points: A transplanted kidney is usually placed in the iliac fossa, its artery and vein joined to the external iliac vessels and its ureter to the bladder; the patient’s own kidneys are usually left in place.
A liver transplant needs joins of the hepatic artery, portal vein, hepatic venous outflow and bile duct; living donors give a part of the liver chosen by its segmental anatomy.
A transplanted heart has no nerve supply, so its rate responds to circulating hormones rather than to the autonomic nerves.
Variations, such as more than one renal artery, are mapped by imaging before surgery.

topics.title: Oncological Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy that explains how cancers spread and how they are staged and treated.
points: Tumours spread by direct invasion, through lymphatics, through the blood and across body cavities.
Lymphatic drainage predicts nodal spread: breast cancer to the axillary nodes, testicular cancer to the para-aortic nodes rather than the inguinal nodes.
Sentinel lymph node biopsy removes the first node that drains a tumour to find out whether the cancer has spread.
Venous drainage predicts blood-borne spread: gut cancers to the liver through the portal vein; the valveless vertebral venous plexus lets prostate cancer reach the spine.

topics.title: Trauma Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy behind the assessment and treatment of injury.
points: Injured patients are assessed in order: airway with cervical spine protection, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure (ABCDE).
A tension pneumothorax in an adult is decompressed in the 4th or 5th intercostal space just in front of the mid-axillary line; the 2nd space in the mid-clavicular line is an alternative.
Pelvic fractures can bleed heavily from the pelvic venous plexuses and branches of the internal iliac arteries; a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters helps control it.
Fractures can injure nearby nerves and vessels: a supracondylar fracture of the humerus can damage the brachial artery and the median nerve.

topics.title: Sports Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of athletic movement and of the injuries that sport causes.
points: The anterior cruciate ligament tears typically in a non-contact pivot on a planted foot; the Lachman and anterior drawer tests examine it.
Inversion sprains of the ankle damage the lateral ligament, most often the anterior talofibular ligament.

The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon usually ruptures 2 to 6 cm above its insertion, where its blood supply is poorest; squeezing the calf then fails to plantarflex the foot (Simmonds’ or Thompson’s test).
Overuse injuries such as tendinopathy and stress fractures develop when load exceeds the tissue’s capacity to adapt.

topics.title: Rehabilitation Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy used to restore movement and function after injury or illness.
points: Knowing each muscle’s action and nerve supply lets therapists target weak muscles and protect healing tissue.
Nerve injuries give recognisable patterns that guide splinting and exercise: radial nerve injury causes wrist drop, common fibular nerve injury causes foot drop.
After a stroke, upper motor neurone signs (weakness, spasticity, brisk reflexes) shape the goals of rehabilitation.
Bone, tendon and muscle remodel in response to load, so loading is increased step by step.

topics.title: Ergonomic Anatomy
topics.summary: Anatomy applied to work, tools and posture to prevent strain and injury.
points: Lifting with the load close to the body, the knees bent and the back upright reduces the load on the lumbar discs.
Repeated wrist flexion, forceful gripping and vibration are risk factors for carpal tunnel syndrome.
A screen at eye level, elbows at about 90 degrees and supported feet reduce neck and back strain at a desk.
Regular changes of position matter as much as any single “correct” posture.

topics.title: Anaesthesia Block Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy used to place local anaesthetic around nerves so that a region of the body is numb (regional anaesthesia).
points: Nerves are blocked where their position is predictable, now usually under ultrasound guidance.
An interscalene block targets the brachial plexus between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius; it almost always blocks the phrenic nerve on the same side too.
A femoral nerve block is placed in the groin, lateral to the femoral artery.
Spinal anaesthesia is injected into the subarachnoid space below the end of the spinal cord (at L3–L4 or L4–L5); epidural anaesthesia into the epidural space outside the dura.

topics.title: Vascular Access Anatomy
topics.summary: Where needles, cannulas and catheters can safely enter veins and arteries.
points: Peripheral cannulas go into the veins on the back of the hand, the cephalic vein at the wrist or the median cubital vein at the elbow.
Central venous catheters go into the internal jugular vein (lateral to the common carotid artery), the subclavian vein or the femoral vein (medial to the femoral artery).
Arterial lines are usually placed in the radial artery at the wrist, after checking that the ulnar artery supplies the hand well.
Ultrasound guidance reduces complications such as arterial puncture and pneumothorax.

topics.title: Endovascular Anatomy
topics.summary: The vascular anatomy needed for procedures carried out inside vessels through catheters: angioplasty, stenting and coiling.
points: The common femoral artery is a usual entry point because it lies over the femoral head, against which it can be compressed afterwards; the radial artery is now widely used for coronary procedures.
Endovascular repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm needs a suitable length of normal aorta below the renal arteries and iliac arteries wide enough for the device.
Coronary angiography shows the left main stem, the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries and the right coronary artery.
Variants such as an aberrant right subclavian artery can make catheter routes difficult.

topics.title: Interventional Radiology Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy behind minimally invasive, image-guided procedures such as biopsies, drains and embolisation.
points: Needle paths are planned to avoid the pleura, bowel and large vessels.
A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) joins a hepatic vein to a branch of the portal vein through the liver to relieve portal hypertension.
Embolisation blocks a chosen artery, for example to stop bleeding from pelvic arteries after trauma or to shrink uterine fibroids through the uterine arteries.
Knowledge of collateral circulation predicts whether tissue will survive when an artery is blocked.

topics.title: Radiation Oncology Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy used to aim radiotherapy at a tumour while sparing the tissues around it.
points: Targets are drawn on CT: the gross tumour volume (GTV), the clinical target volume (CTV, adding likely microscopic spread) and the planning target volume (PTV, adding a margin for movement and set-up).
Nearby organs at risk, such as the spinal cord, parotid glands, rectum and heart, have dose limits.
Lymph node regions are drawn using published anatomical atlases.
Breathing moves tumours in the lower chest and upper abdomen; breath-hold and gating reduce the margins needed.

topics.title: Robotic Surgery Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy as seen and handled through a surgical robot: a magnified 3D view and wristed instruments through small ports.
points: It is widely used in the narrow pelvis, for prostatectomy, hysterectomy and rectal surgery.
Most systems give little or no sense of touch, so surgeons rely on visual landmarks, such as the neurovascular bundles beside the prostate.
Port positions are planned around the target organ and the patient’s body shape.
The magnified view helps preserve small nerves and vessels.

topics.title: Somite Differentiation
topics.summary: How the paired blocks of paraxial mesoderm beside the neural tube become the vertebrae, muscles and dermis.
points: Somites appear from about day 20; around 42 to 44 pairs form, and some at the tail end later disappear.
Each somite divides into the sclerotome (vertebrae and ribs), the myotome (skeletal muscle) and the dermatome (dermis of the back).
Each vertebra forms from the lower half of one sclerotome and the upper half of the next, so spinal nerves come to lie between the vertebrae.
This segmental origin explains the dermatome and myotome maps of the adult body.

topics.title: Limb Bud Development
topics.summary: How the limbs grow out from the body wall and are patterned along three axes.
points: The upper limb buds appear at the end of week 4, the lower limb buds a day or two later.
The apical ectodermal ridge drives growth from the shoulder to the fingertips; the zone of polarising activity (Sonic hedgehog) sets the thumb-to-little-finger axis.
The digits separate by programmed cell death (apoptosis) between them; failure gives fused digits (syndactyly).
The upper limbs rotate laterally and the lower limbs medially by about 90 degrees, so the elbow points back and the knee forwards.

topics.title: Craniofacial Development
topics.summary: How the face, palate and skull form, mainly in weeks 4 to 12.
points: The face forms from five prominences around the primitive mouth: the frontonasal prominence and the paired maxillary and mandibular prominences.
Neural crest cells form much of the skeleton and connective tissue of the face.
The upper lip forms from the medial nasal and maxillary prominences; failure to fuse causes cleft lip.
The palatal shelves grow from the maxillary prominences and fuse in the midline; failure causes cleft palate.

topics.title: Cardiovascular Embryology
topics.summary: How the heart and great vessels form, the first organ system to work in the embryo.
points: The heart starts as a tube that begins to beat at about day 22.
The tube loops to the right, and septa divide the atria, ventricles and outflow tract into two parallel circulations.
The spiral aorticopulmonary septum, built with neural crest cells, divides the outflow tract; faults cause transposition of the great arteries or tetralogy of Fallot.
Ventricular septal defect is the most common congenital heart defect.

topics.title: Respiratory Embryology
topics.summary: How the airways and lungs grow from the foregut.
points: The lung bud grows from the ventral wall of the foregut in week 4.
The tracheo-oesophageal septum separates the trachea from the oesophagus; faults cause oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
The lungs pass through embryonic, pseudoglandular, canalicular, saccular and alveolar stages; alveoli go on forming after birth.
Type II pneumocytes make surfactant from about week 20; babies born too early without enough of it develop respiratory distress syndrome.

topics.title: Gastrointestinal Embryology
topics.summary: How the gut tube forms, rotates and acquires its blood supply.
points: The primitive gut has three parts: the foregut, midgut and hindgut, supplied by the coeliac trunk and the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries.
The midgut herniates into the umbilical cord in week 6, rotates 270 degrees anticlockwise around the superior mesenteric artery and returns by week 10.
Malrotation can lead to volvulus; failure of the gut to return causes exomphalos (omphalocele).
A remnant of the vitelline duct forms a Meckel’s diverticulum in about 2% of people.

topics.title: Urogenital Embryology
topics.summary: How the kidneys, urinary tract and reproductive organs develop from the intermediate mesoderm.
points: Three kidneys form in turn: the pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros, which becomes the permanent kidney.
The ureteric bud forms the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts; the metanephric blastema forms the nephrons.
The kidneys ascend from the pelvis; a horseshoe kidney is held low by the inferior mesenteric artery.
The gonads are indifferent until about week 7, when the SRY gene on the Y chromosome directs the formation of testes.

topics.title: Endocrine Embryology
topics.summary: How the endocrine glands form and why some end up far from where they began.
points: The thyroid starts at the foramen caecum of the tongue and descends along the thyroglossal duct; remnants can form a midline thyroglossal cyst.
The anterior pituitary comes from Rathke’s pouch in the roof of the mouth; the posterior pituitary grows down from the diencephalon.
The inferior parathyroids and the thymus come from the third pharyngeal pouch; the superior parathyroids from the fourth.
The adrenal cortex comes from mesoderm and the adrenal medulla from neural crest.

topics.title: Ocular and Otic Embryology
topics.summary: How the eye and the ear develop.
points: The optic vesicle grows out from the forebrain and induces the lens; the optic cup forms the retina.
Failure of the optic fissure to close leaves a gap in the iris or retina (coloboma).
The inner ear forms from the otic placode; the malleus and incus come from the first pharyngeal arch and the stapes from the second.
The external acoustic meatus comes from the first pharyngeal cleft, and the auricle from small swellings (hillocks) around it.

topics.title: Integumentary Embryology
topics.summary: How the skin and its appendages develop.
points: The epidermis comes from surface ectoderm and the dermis from mesoderm.
Melanocytes migrate into the skin from the neural crest.
Hair follicles, sweat glands and mammary glands grow down from the epidermis; the mammary ridges run from axilla to groin, which explains extra nipples.
The nails form at the tips of the digits from about week 10.

topics.title: Twin and Multiple Gestation Embryology
topics.summary: How twins form and how the timing of division sets their membranes and placentas.
points: Dizygotic twins come from two separately fertilised eggs and always have two amnions and two chorions, though the placentas may fuse.
Monozygotic twins come from one zygote that splits; the timing of the split decides how membranes are shared.
Split by day 3: two chorions and two amnions; days 4 to 8: one chorion, two amnions; days 8 to 12: one chorion, one amnion; later: conjoined twins.
Monochorionic twins share placental circulation and can develop twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

topics.title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Dynamics
topics.summary: How cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is made, circulates and is absorbed.
points: About 500 mL is made each day, mostly by the choroid plexuses; about 150 mL is present at any time.

It flows from the lateral ventricles through the interventricular foramina, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct and fourth ventricle, then out through the median and lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space.
It is absorbed into the dural venous sinuses through the arachnoid granulations.
A block in the pathway causes obstructive hydrocephalus; poor absorption causes communicating hydrocephalus.

topics.title: Blood-Brain Barrier
topics.summary: The barrier that controls what passes from the blood into the brain.
points: It is formed by brain capillary endothelial cells joined by tight junctions, with their basement membrane, pericytes and astrocyte end-feet.
Water, gases and fat-soluble substances cross freely; glucose and amino acids need carriers.
It shields neurons from changes in blood composition, but also keeps out many drugs.
Its breakdown in tumours, infection or stroke causes oedema and makes lesions enhance with contrast on scans.

topics.title: Circumventricular Organs
topics.summary: Small areas around the ventricles where the blood–brain barrier is absent, so the brain can sense the blood and secrete into it.
points: Their capillaries are fenestrated.
Sensory organs, such as the area postrema, subfornical organ and organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis, sample the blood.
Secretory organs, such as the posterior pituitary, median eminence and pineal gland, release hormones into the blood.
The area postrema in the floor of the fourth ventricle is the chemoreceptor trigger zone for vomiting.

topics.title: Reticular Formation
topics.summary: A network of neurons running through the core of the brainstem.
points: Its ascending reticular activating system keeps the cortex awake and alert.
It contains centres that help control breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.
Reticulospinal tracts from it adjust posture and muscle tone.
Damage to the reticular activating system can cause coma.

topics.title: Hypothalamic-Pituitary Axis
topics.summary: The link through which the hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland and, through it, many other endocrine glands.
points: The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary through releasing hormones carried in the hypophyseal portal veins, and the posterior pituitary through nerve fibres.
The anterior pituitary makes growth hormone, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH.
The posterior pituitary releases antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus.
Pituitary tumours can press on the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia) and disturb hormone levels.

topics.title: Extrapyramidal System
topics.summary: The motor pathways other than the corticospinal tract, which shape posture, muscle tone and automatic movement.
points: It involves the basal ganglia, cerebellum and brainstem nuclei, with the reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, rubrospinal and tectospinal tracts.
The basal ganglia act mainly through loops back to the motor cortex via the thalamus.
Parkinson’s disease follows loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra: tremor, rigidity and slowness of movement.
Huntington’s disease damages the caudate nucleus and putamen and causes involuntary jerky movements (chorea).

topics.title: Pyramidal System
topics.summary: The corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, which carry signals for voluntary movement from the cortex.
points: Fibres start mainly in the motor cortex of the precentral gyrus and pass through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncles and medullary pyramids.
About 85 to 90% of corticospinal fibres cross in the decussation of the pyramids and form the lateral corticospinal tract.
Upper motor neurone lesions cause weakness, spasticity, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response.
Lower motor neurone lesions cause flaccid weakness, wasting, fasciculation and reduced reflexes.

topics.title: Somatosensory Pathways
topics.summary: The pathways that carry touch, vibration, proprioception, pain and temperature from the body to the cortex.
points: The dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception and crosses in the medulla.
The spinothalamic (anterolateral) pathway carries pain, temperature and crude touch and crosses in the spinal cord within a segment or two.
Both relay in the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus and end in the postcentral gyrus.
Hemisection of the cord (Brown-Séquard syndrome) loses proprioception and vibration on the same side and pain and temperature on the opposite side below the lesion.

topics.title: Pain and Temperature Pathways
topics.summary: How painful and thermal stimuli reach consciousness.
points: Free nerve endings detect them; thinly myelinated Aδ fibres carry sharp, fast pain and unmyelinated C fibres dull, slow pain.
The first neurons synapse in the dorsal horn; the second cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the lateral spinothalamic tract.
From the face, pain and temperature run in the spinal tract and nucleus of the trigeminal nerve.
Referred pain arises when visceral and somatic fibres converge on the same spinal segments, as in heart pain felt in the left arm.

topics.title: Proprioceptive Pathways
topics.summary: The pathways that tell the brain where the body’s parts are and how they move.
points: Muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs and joint receptors provide the signals.
Conscious proprioception ascends in the dorsal columns and medial lemniscus to the cortex.
Unconscious proprioception reaches the cerebellum through the spinocerebellar and cuneocerebellar tracts.
Loss of proprioception causes sensory ataxia, with unsteadiness that worsens when the eyes are closed (positive Romberg’s test).

topics.title: Olfactory Pathway
topics.summary: The pathway of smell, from the nose to the brain.
points: Olfactory receptor neurons in the roof of the nasal cavity send axons through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb.
The olfactory tract runs to the piriform cortex, amygdala and entorhinal cortex.
Smell is the only sense that reaches the cortex without first relaying in the thalamus.
A fracture of the cribriform plate can cause loss of smell (anosmia) and leakage of CSF from the nose.

topics.title: Gustatory Pathway
topics.summary: The pathway of taste, from the taste buds to the cortex.
points: Taste buds lie mainly on the tongue, with others on the palate and epiglottis.
The facial nerve (chorda tympani) carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, the glossopharyngeal nerve from the posterior third and the vagus from the epiglottis.
All taste fibres end in the nucleus of the solitary tract and relay in the ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus to the insula and frontal operculum.
The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

topics.title: Oculomotor Control Systems
topics.summary: The nerves and brain centres that move the eyes together.
points: The oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV) and abducens (VI) nerves supply the extraocular muscles.
The medial longitudinal fasciculus links their nuclei; damage to it causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia, classically in multiple sclerosis.
Fast eye movements (saccades) are driven by the frontal eye fields and brainstem gaze centres; smooth pursuit involves the parieto-occipital cortex and cerebellum.
The vestibulo-ocular reflex keeps the gaze steady when the head moves.

topics.title: Autonomic Plexuses
topics.summary: Networks of sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres around the organs and the large vessels.
points: In the thorax, the cardiac, pulmonary and oesophageal plexuses.
In the abdomen, the coeliac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric plexuses along the branches of the aorta.
In the pelvis, the superior and inferior hypogastric plexuses supply the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs.
A coeliac plexus block can relieve the pain of pancreatic cancer.

topics.title: Veterinary Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of domestic and other animals, studied for animal health and welfare.
points: It uses its own terminology (Nomina Anatomica Veterinaria) and terms for four-legged animals: cranial, caudal, dorsal, ventral and rostral.
Ruminants such as cattle and sheep have a stomach of four compartments: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum.
The horse has no gallbladder and a very large caecum for fermenting fibre.
Comparative knowledge supports the control of diseases shared between animals and humans.

topics.title: Zootomy
topics.summary: The dissection and anatomy of animals: the older name for comparative animal anatomy.
points: Aristotle described animal structure from dissection in the 4th century BCE.
Galen’s human anatomy was largely based on the dissection of monkeys and other animals, which explains several of his errors.
Comparing animals revealed homologous structures and helped classify animals by body plan.
Today the term is mostly historical; imaging and molecular methods have joined dissection.

topics.title: Phytotomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of plants: the study of their cells and tissues.
points: Plant tissues are grouped as dermal (epidermis), ground (parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma) and vascular (xylem and phloem).
Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots; phloem carries sugars from the leaves.
Plant cells, unlike animal cells, have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole.
Nehemiah Grew and Marcello Malpighi founded plant anatomy with the microscope in the 17th century.

topics.title: Invertebrate Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of animals without a vertebral column, which make up the great majority of animal species.
points: Body plans range from radial symmetry (cnidarians such as jellyfish) to bilateral symmetry (worms, molluscs and arthropods).
Arthropods have an outer skeleton (exoskeleton) of chitin and jointed limbs; insects have an open circulation.
Many molluscs have a muscular foot, a mantle and often a shell.
Model invertebrates, such as the fruit fly Drosophila and the nematode C. elegans, revealed genes that also pattern the human body.

topics.title: Vertebrate Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy shared, and varied, across animals with a vertebral column.
points: Shared features include a vertebral column around the spinal cord, a skull, a notochord in the embryo and pharyngeal arches.
The groups are fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
The heart ranges from two chambers in fish to four in birds and mammals.
Homologous structures, such as the forelimb bones of a human arm, a bat’s wing and a whale’s flipper, show common descent.

topics.title: Primatology Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of primates, the group that includes humans.
points: Primates have grasping hands, nails instead of claws, forward-facing eyes with depth perception and large brains for their body size.
The great apes (orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos) are the closest living relatives of humans.
Humans are adapted to walking upright: an S-shaped spine, a bowl-shaped pelvis, an angled femur and an arched foot with a big toe in line with the others.
Primate anatomy informs the study of human evolution.

topics.title: Palaeoanatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of extinct organisms, reconstructed from fossils.
points: Fossil bones, teeth and footprints reveal body size, posture and way of moving; CT scanning shows internal structures such as the brain case.
Fossils such as Australopithecus afarensis (“Lucy”, about 3.2 million years old) show upright walking long before the brain enlarged.
Palaeopathology studies disease and injury in ancient remains.
Comparing fossils with living species traces how structures changed over time.

topics.title: History of Anatomy
topics.summary: How knowledge of the body grew from ancient dissection to modern imaging.
points: Herophilus and Erasistratus dissected human bodies in Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE; Galen’s teaching, based largely on animals, dominated for more than 1,300 years.
Andreas Vesalius corrected Galen through human dissection in De humani corporis fabrica (1543).
William Harvey described the circulation of the blood in 1628.
The Anatomy Act 1832 regulated the supply of bodies in Britain; the 19th century produced great atlases, and the 20th added radiological and microscopic anatomy.

topics.title: Anatomical Nomenclature and Terminologia Anatomica
topics.summary: The international system of anatomical names.
points: Terminologia Anatomica (first edition 1998, second edition 2019) is the international standard, with Latin terms and English equivalents.
It is prepared by the Federative International Programme for Anatomical Terminology (FIPAT) of the International Federation of Associations of Anatomists.
Eponyms are discouraged in favour of descriptive names: “pharyngotympanic tube” rather than “Eustachian tube”.
Precise, shared names prevent errors between clinicians and across languages.

topics.title: Body Donation Ethics
topics.summary: The ethics and law of giving one’s body for anatomical teaching and research.
points: Donation must rest on informed, freely given consent made by the donor during life.
In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the Human Tissue Act 2004 and the Human Tissue Authority regulate donation and anatomical examination; Scotland has its own Act (2006).
Donors are treated with dignity, and many medical schools hold services of thanksgiving.
Past abuses, such as body snatching and the use of executed prisoners, led to today’s regulation.

topics.title: Anatomical Museum Curation
topics.summary: The care, documentation and display of anatomical specimens.
points: Collections include wet specimens in fixative, dry bones, plastinated specimens and models.
Good curation records consent and provenance and displays human remains respectfully; some remains of uncertain origin have been returned to their communities.
In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, public display of human tissue from people who died less than 100 years ago needs a Human Tissue Authority licence.
Collections such as the Hunterian in London continue to support teaching and research.

topics.title: Forensic Osteology
topics.summary: The analysis of skeletal remains for legal investigations.
points: A biological profile estimates sex (mainly from the pelvis and skull), age at death (growth plate fusion, pubic symphysis, teeth), stature (long bone lengths) and ancestry.
Healing shows injury before death; fresh fractures without healing suggest injury around the time of death.
Changes after death, from weathering or animals, must be told apart from injury.
Identity is confirmed with dental records, healed fractures, surgical implants or DNA.

topics.title: Somatotyping
topics.summary: A method of describing body shape by three components.
points: William Sheldon introduced it; Heath and Carter later turned it into a measurement-based method.
Endomorphy rates relative fatness, mesomorphy musculoskeletal robustness and ectomorphy linearity.
The Heath–Carter method calculates each rating from height, weight, skinfolds, bone breadths and limb girths.
It is used in sport science; Sheldon’s claimed links between body shape and personality are discredited.

topics.title: Anthropometry
topics.summary: The standardised measurement of the human body.
points: It includes height, weight, segment lengths, circumferences, breadths and skinfold thickness.
Body mass index is weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres; waist circumference reflects abdominal fat.
It underpins growth charts, nutrition assessment, ergonomic design and sport science.
Standard landmarks and protocols make measurements repeatable between observers.

topics.title: Topographic Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of each region described by the position and relations of its structures.
points: Structures are described by their relations: in front of, behind, medial or lateral to their neighbours.
Surface projections link deep structures to the skin: the transpyloric plane (L1) crosses the pylorus, the neck of the pancreas, the hila of the kidneys and the fundus of the gallbladder.
It is the basis of surgical approaches, needle placement and the interpretation of imaging.
In many curricula it is taught together with regional anatomy.

topics.title: Living Anatomy
topics.summary: Anatomy studied in the living person through inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation and imaging.
points: Students learn surface landmarks by examining each other.
Living anatomy moves: the diaphragm and the organs under it descend as you breathe in, and posture changes the position of organs.
It includes testing movements and muscles and feeling pulses.
Ultrasound shows structures moving in real time without radiation.

topics.title: Artistic Anatomy
topics.summary: Anatomy for artists: the bones and muscles that shape the visible form of the body.
points: Leonardo da Vinci made detailed anatomical drawings from dissection in the early 16th century.
The woodcuts of Vesalius’s Fabrica (1543) came from artists associated with Titian’s workshop.
Artists use proportions, such as an adult being about seven and a half to eight heads tall.
Surface landmarks such as the clavicle, sternocleidomastoid and iliac crest shape the figure.

topics.title: Forensic Anatomy
topics.summary: Anatomy applied to the law: identification, injury and the cause and timing of death.
points: It includes forensic osteology, forensic odontology and the interpretation of wounds.
Injury patterns, such as defence wounds on the forearms, help reconstruct events.
Changes after death (rigor mortis, livor mortis and cooling) help estimate the time of death.
Comparison with medical and dental records confirms identity.

topics.title: Anthropological Anatomy
topics.summary: The study of human anatomical variation between populations and over time.
points: Stature, body proportions and skin pigmentation vary with climate and ancestry.
Bergmann’s rule (larger bodies in colder climates) and Allen’s rule (shorter limbs in colder climates) describe some of these patterns.
Skeletons record activity, diet and disease.
It draws on anthropometry and osteology.

topics.title: Evolutionary Anatomy
topics.summary: Explaining the structure of the body by its evolutionary history.
points: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch because it developed with the sixth pharyngeal arch artery, which became the ductus arteriosus.
Walking upright reshaped the spine, pelvis and foot, with costs such as low back pain and a difficult birth.
Vestigial structures, such as the coccyx and the plica semilunaris of the eye, are remnants of features in our ancestors.
A shortened jaw leaves too little room for the third molars, which often fail to erupt.

topics.title: Geriatric Anatomy
topics.summary: The changes in the body’s structure that come with ageing.
points: Bone mass falls (osteoporosis) and muscle mass and strength decline (sarcopenia).
Intervertebral discs lose water and height, and articular cartilage thins.
Skin thins and loses elasticity; arteries stiffen, which raises systolic blood pressure.
The lens stiffens (presbyopia) and hearing of high frequencies declines (presbycusis).

topics.title: Paediatric Anatomy
topics.summary: How a child’s body differs from an adult’s: children are not small adults.
points: Infants have a relatively large head, short neck and large tongue; the larynx sits higher (about C3–C4) and the epiglottis is floppier.
Growth plates are open, so fractures may cross them (Salter–Harris classification); young bones can bend and crack on one side (greenstick fractures).
The posterior fontanelle closes by about 2 to 3 months and the anterior fontanelle by about 18 to 24 months.
Children have a larger body surface area for their weight and lose heat and fluid quickly.

topics.title: Fetal Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of the fetus, from week 9 of development to birth.
points: Organs formed in the embryonic period now grow and mature.
The fetal circulation bypasses the lungs through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, and partly bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus.
The lungs are filled with fluid and do not exchange gases until birth.
The routine anomaly scan, at about 18 to 21 weeks, checks the fetal anatomy.

topics.title: Neonatal Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of the newborn in the first 28 days and the changes at birth.
points: At the first breaths the lungs expand, pulmonary resistance falls and the foramen ovale closes as left atrial pressure rises.
The ductus arteriosus closes within days and later becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
A large surface area for body weight means rapid heat loss; brown fat produces heat.
The skull bones are separated by sutures and fontanelles, which allowed the head to mould during birth.

topics.title: Dental Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of the teeth and the tissues that support them.
points: There are 20 primary (deciduous) teeth and 32 permanent teeth.
Each quadrant of the permanent dentition has two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars.
A tooth is made of enamel, dentine, pulp and cementum and is held in its socket by the periodontal ligament.
The upper teeth are supplied by the superior alveolar nerves (V2) and the lower teeth by the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), the target of the inferior alveolar nerve block.

topics.title: Oral Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of the mouth: lips, cheeks, gums, teeth, tongue, palate, floor of the mouth and salivary glands.
points: The parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar; the submandibular ducts open beside the frenulum of the tongue.
Mylohyoid forms the muscular floor of the mouth.
The tongue is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (motor) and by the lingual, chorda tympani and glossopharyngeal nerves (sensation and taste).
Oral cancers arise most often on the side of the tongue and the floor of the mouth.

topics.title: Ocular Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of the eye and its surrounding structures.
points: The eyeball has three coats: fibrous (sclera and cornea), vascular (choroid, ciliary body and iris) and neural (retina).
The cornea provides most of the eye’s focusing power; the lens adjusts it for near vision (accommodation) as the ciliary muscle contracts.
The fovea of the macula holds only cones and gives the sharpest vision; the optic disc has no photoreceptors and forms the blind spot.
Aqueous humour drains through the trabecular meshwork into the scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm); poor drainage raises pressure in the eye (glaucoma).

topics.title: Otological Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of the ear that matters in ear disease and ear surgery.
points: The facial nerve runs through the temporal bone close to the middle ear and can be injured by surgery or fractures.
Middle ear infection can spread to the mastoid air cells (mastoiditis).
The pharyngotympanic tube is shorter and more horizontal in children, one reason middle ear infection is common in them.
The chorda tympani crosses the tympanic membrane on its inner side, so ear surgery can alter taste.

topics.title: Gynaecological Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of the female reproductive organs, as used in gynaecology.
points: The uterus is usually anteverted and anteflexed; the pelvic floor and the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments support it.
The uterine artery, from the internal iliac artery, crosses above the ureter beside the cervix.
Lymph from the ovaries drains with the ovarian vessels to the para-aortic nodes; lymph from the cervix drains to the pelvic nodes.
The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is the lowest point of the female peritoneal cavity, where fluid and blood collect.

topics.title: Obstetric Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of pregnancy and childbirth.
points: The pelvic inlet is widest from side to side and the outlet from front to back, so the baby’s head rotates as it descends.
The fetal skull moulds at its sutures and fontanelles.
An episiotomy is cut mediolaterally to avoid the anal sphincter.
A pudendal nerve block, near the ischial spine, numbs the perineum.

topics.title: Urological Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of the urinary tract and the male genital organs, as used in urology.
points: Ureteric stones lodge at three narrow points: the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and the vesicoureteric junction.
The prostate surrounds the first part of the urethra; benign enlargement of its transition zone obstructs urine flow, while most cancers arise in the peripheral zone, felt on rectal examination.
The male urethra is about 18 to 20 cm long and the female urethra about 4 cm, one reason urinary infections are commoner in women.
The testes drain to the para-aortic lymph nodes, following their embryological descent.

topics.title: Orthopaedic Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of bones, joints, ligaments and tendons, and of the nerves and vessels at risk in injuries and operations.
points: The femoral head is supplied mainly by the medial circumflex femoral artery; a displaced intracapsular neck fracture risks avascular necrosis.
Nerves at risk include the axillary nerve at the surgical neck of the humerus, the radial nerve on its shaft and the common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula.
Surgical approaches use internervous planes to protect muscle nerve supply.
Growth plates and their fractures matter in children.

topics.title: Neurosurgical Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of the brain, spine, nerves and their coverings, as used in neurosurgery.
points: The pterion overlies the middle meningeal artery, which bleeds in an extradural haematoma.
Tearing of bridging veins between the cortex and the dural sinuses causes a subdural haematoma.
Kocher’s point, in front of the coronal suture, is a standard entry point for draining the lateral ventricle.
Spinal surgery depends on the relations of the pedicles, nerve roots and spinal cord.

topics.title: Endoscopic Anatomy
topics.summary: The appearance of hollow organs seen from the inside through an endoscope.
points: In upper gastrointestinal endoscopy the gastro-oesophageal junction lies about 40 cm from the incisor teeth.
Colonoscopy passes the rectum, sigmoid and descending colon, the splenic flexure, the transverse colon, the hepatic flexure and the ascending colon to the caecum.
The caecum is confirmed by the appendiceal orifice and the ileocaecal valve.
Bronchoscopy shows the carina and the openings of the lobar and segmental bronchi.

topics.title: Laparoscopic Anatomy
topics.summary: Abdominal and pelvic anatomy as seen through a camera, with the abdomen inflated with carbon dioxide.
points: Ports are placed to avoid the inferior epigastric vessels, which run up behind the rectus abdominis.
In laparoscopic cholecystectomy the cystic duct and cystic artery are shown clearly in the hepatocystic (Calot’s) triangle before anything is divided (the critical view of safety).
Without touch, surgeons rely on visual landmarks.
The view is magnified, so small vessels and nerves can be identified and preserved.

topics.title: Microsurgical Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy of small vessels and nerves repaired under an operating microscope.
points: Free flaps move tissue with its own artery and vein, which are joined to vessels at the new site; breast reconstruction often uses a flap based on the deep inferior epigastric vessels.
Nerves are repaired by joining their outer sheath (epineurium) or their fascicles.
After repair, axons regrow at roughly 1 mm a day.
Replanting a finger needs repair of bone, tendons, arteries, veins and nerves.

topics.title: Molecular Anatomy
topics.summary: Mapping where genes and proteins are found within tissues and cells.
points: Techniques include immunohistochemistry, in situ hybridisation and spatial transcriptomics.
It explains how cell types differ even when they look alike under the microscope.
Large projects such as the Human Cell Atlas catalogue cell types across the body.
It links structure to function and to the mechanisms of disease.

topics.title: Ultrastructural Anatomy
topics.summary: The fine structure of cells and tissues, seen with the electron microscope.
points: It shows organelles: mitochondria, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and lysosomes.
Tight junctions seal neighbouring cells, adherens junctions and desmosomes anchor them, and gap junctions connect their cytoplasm.
Basement membranes, cilia and microvilli can be studied in detail.
It helps diagnose some kidney, muscle and ciliary diseases.

topics.title: Immunohistochemical Anatomy
topics.summary: Mapping specific proteins in tissues with labelled antibodies.
points: Marker proteins identify cell types, such as cytokeratins in epithelium, desmin in muscle and GFAP in astrocytes.
In tumours it reveals the tissue of origin of a metastasis and tests hormone receptors and HER2 in breast cancer.
In the nervous system it maps neurotransmitters and their receptors.
Positive and negative controls are needed to trust the result.

topics.title: Digital Anatomy
topics.summary: Anatomy recorded, stored and taught with digital media: scans, 3D models and software.
points: The Visible Human Project (1994–1995) produced full cross-sectional image sets of a male and a female body.
CT and MRI data can be reconstructed into 3D models.
Digital atlases and annotated images support self-study.
It complements, rather than replaces, dissection and clinical examination.

topics.title: Virtual Anatomy
topics.summary: Learning anatomy through interactive 3D models and virtual or augmented reality.
points: Learners can rotate structures, peel away layers and cut sections, as in this app’s 3D body.
Virtual dissection tables show life-size reconstructions from medical images.
It allows unlimited repetition without specimens.
Studies suggest it works best combined with other methods.

topics.title: 3D Computational Anatomy
topics.summary: The computational analysis of anatomical shape and its variation from medical images.
