points: It uses image segmentation, image registration and statistical shape models.
Applications include surgical planning, patient-specific 3D-printed models and measuring brain atrophy.
Finite element models predict the stresses in bones and implants.
Population atlases describe normal variation and detect abnormal shapes.

topics.title: Quantitative Anatomy
topics.summary: Measuring anatomical features: lengths, areas, volumes and numbers of cells.
points: Normal ranges help define disease, for example of heart chamber size or organ volume.
It uses morphometric and stereological methods.
Statistics account for variation between individuals.
Measurements must be standardised to be compared between studies.

topics.title: Morphometrics
topics.summary: The quantitative analysis of form: size and shape.
points: Traditional morphometrics uses distances, angles and ratios.
Geometric morphometrics uses the coordinates of landmarks and Procrustes superimposition to compare shape independently of size.
It is used in evolutionary biology, forensic science and craniofacial research.
Results are often shown as shape changes along statistical axes of variation.

topics.title: Stereology
topics.summary: Estimating three-dimensional quantities, such as volume, surface area and number, from two-dimensional sections.
points: The Cavalieri principle estimates the volume of an object from evenly spaced sections.
The optical disector counts cells without bias from their size or shape.
Unbiased results need systematic uniform random sampling.
It is widely used to count neurons and to measure organ volumes.

topics.title: Cadaveric Dissection
topics.summary: Learning anatomy by dissecting bodies donated for that purpose.
points: It shows three-dimensional relations, real variation and the texture of tissues.
Bodies are usually embalmed with formaldehyde-based fluids; Thiel embalming and fresh-frozen bodies keep tissues more lifelike.
It teaches teamwork, professionalism and respect for donors.
Gloves, good ventilation and care with sharp instruments and fixatives keep it safe.

topics.title: Prosection Study
topics.summary: Studying specimens that have already been dissected by an expert (a prosector).
points: It saves time and displays structures clearly.
Specimens can be reused for many students.
It offers less hands-on discovery than dissection.
It is often combined with models, imaging and surface anatomy.

topics.title: Plastination Study
topics.summary: Learning from specimens preserved by plastination.
points: Gunther von Hagens developed plastination in 1977.
Water and fat are replaced by acetone and then, under vacuum, by silicone or epoxy resin, which is then hardened.
The specimens are dry, odourless, durable and safe to handle.
Thin plastinated slices compare well with CT and MRI sections.

topics.title: Histological Slide Preparation
topics.summary: How tissue is turned into thin, stained sections for the light microscope.
points: Tissue is fixed (usually in 10% neutral buffered formalin), dehydrated in alcohol, cleared in xylene and embedded in paraffin wax.
A microtome cuts sections about 3 to 5 micrometres thick.
Haematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple and eosin stains cytoplasm pink (H&E).
Frozen sections give a quick answer during surgery.

topics.title: Histochemistry
topics.summary: Using chemical reactions to show particular substances in tissue sections.
points: Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stains glycogen and mucins magenta.
Masson’s trichrome shows collagen; Perls’ Prussian blue shows iron.
Congo red shows amyloid, which gives apple-green birefringence in polarised light.
Enzyme histochemistry shows enzyme activity in frozen tissue, for example in muscle biopsies.

topics.title: Immunohistochemistry
topics.summary: Showing specific proteins in tissue with antibodies.
points: An antibody binds its target antigen and is made visible with an enzyme that produces a coloured product (often brown) or with a fluorescent label.
The indirect method uses a labelled secondary antibody to amplify the signal.
Positive and negative controls are essential.
It is used in diagnosis, for example to classify tumours or test HER2, and in research.

topics.title: Electron Microscopy
topics.summary: Imaging with electrons, which gives far higher resolution than light.
points: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images thin sections and shows internal structure.
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images surfaces with a three-dimensional appearance.
Tissue is fixed in glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide and embedded in resin.
It helps diagnose kidney diseases, some muscle and nerve diseases and disorders of cilia.

topics.title: Live Ultrasound Scanning
topics.summary: Using ultrasound to see living anatomy in real time.
points: Sound waves reflect from boundaries between tissues to build the image.
Higher frequencies give better resolution but penetrate less, so linear high-frequency probes are used for superficial structures.
Fluid appears black (anechoic); bone and gas block the beam.
Scanning the heart, neck vessels, abdomen and muscles teaches anatomy safely, without radiation.

topics.title: Cross-Sectional Correlation
topics.summary: Matching anatomy in sections to CT and MRI images.
points: Axial images are viewed as if from the patient’s feet, so the patient’s right is on the viewer’s left.
Images are cut in axial, coronal and sagittal planes.
Studying sectioned specimens alongside scans builds a three-dimensional picture.
Recognising structures in section is the basis of reading scans.

topics.title: Surface Landmark Palpation
topics.summary: Finding deep structures by feeling features on the body’s surface.
points: The sternal angle marks the second costal cartilage, from which the ribs can be counted.
Pulses are felt at the carotid, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries.
The vertebra prominens (C7) is the most prominent spinous process at the base of the neck.
A line joining the tops of the iliac crests crosses the L4 spinous process.

topics.title: Clinical Correlation Studies
topics.summary: Linking anatomy to the signs, symptoms and treatment of disease.
points: Hoarseness after thyroid surgery points to injury of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Wrist drop after a humeral shaft fracture points to the radial nerve.
Case-based learning connects symptoms to the structures involved.
Applying anatomy to cases strengthens memory and clinical reasoning.

topics.title: Levels of Structural Organisation
topics.summary: The levels at which the body is built, from atoms to the whole person.
points: The levels are chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, organ system and organism.
There are four basic tissues: epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.
An organ is made of two or more tissues working together.
Organ systems include the integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, lymphatic, respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive systems.

topics.title: Body Cavities and Membranes
topics.summary: The spaces of the body and the membranes that line them.
points: The dorsal cavity holds the brain and spinal cord; the ventral cavity is divided by the diaphragm into the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities.
Serous membranes (pleura, pericardium and peritoneum) have a parietal and a visceral layer with a thin film of fluid between them.
Mucous membranes line tracts that open to the outside; synovial membranes line joint cavities.
Inflammation of a serous membrane hurts with movement: pleurisy, pericarditis, peritonitis.

topics.title: Fascial Planes and Compartments
topics.summary: The sheets of connective tissue that wrap and divide the body’s soft tissues.
points: Superficial fascia (subcutaneous tissue) lies under the skin; deep fascia surrounds muscles.
Intermuscular septa divide the limbs into compartments, each with its own function and nerve supply.
Fascial planes guide the spread of infection and give surgeons access.
Raised pressure in a compartment causes compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the muscles.

topics.title: Joint Classification and Biomechanics
topics.summary: How joints are classified and how their structure balances movement and stability.
points: Fibrous joints include sutures, syndesmoses and gomphoses; cartilaginous joints are synchondroses and symphyses; the rest are synovial.
Synovial joints are plane, hinge, pivot, condyloid, saddle or ball-and-socket.
Stability comes from bone shape, ligaments and muscles; the shoulder trades stability for mobility, the hip the reverse.
Articular cartilage and synovial fluid give extremely low friction.

topics.title: Vascular Anastomoses and Collateral Circulation
topics.summary: Connections between vessels that give blood alternative routes.
points: The arterial circle at the base of the brain (circle of Willis) joins the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems.
Anastomoses around the elbow, knee and scapula can keep a limb supplied if a main artery is blocked.
Portosystemic anastomoses, such as those at the lower oesophagus, enlarge into varices in portal hypertension.
End arteries, such as the central retinal artery, have no effective anastomoses, so a block causes infarction.

topics.title: Lymphatic Drainage Pathways
topics.summary: The routes by which lymph returns from the tissues to the blood.
points: Lymph flows from lymphatic capillaries through vessels and lymph nodes to the great veins at the root of the neck.
The thoracic duct drains most of the body; the right lymphatic duct drains the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb and the right side of the thorax.
Regional nodes: the head and neck drain to the deep cervical nodes, the upper limb and breast to the axillary nodes, and the lower limb and perineum to the inguinal nodes.
When drainage fails, as after lymph node removal, lymphoedema develops.

topics.title: Autonomic Innervation Pathways
topics.summary: The two-neuron pathways of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.
points: Each pathway has a preganglionic neuron in the central nervous system and a postganglionic neuron in a ganglion.
Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (T1 to L2), with ganglia in the sympathetic trunks or in front of the aorta; most of its endings release noradrenaline.
Parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral (cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X, and S2 to S4), with ganglia near or in the organs; its endings release acetylcholine.
Sweat glands are supplied by sympathetic fibres that release acetylcholine.

topics.title: Somatic Innervation Pathways
topics.summary: The nerves that supply the skin, skeletal muscles and joints.
points: Motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord send axons directly to skeletal muscle.
The dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots join to form each spinal nerve, which divides into dorsal and ventral rami.
Ventral rami form the cervical, brachial, lumbar and sacral plexuses; thoracic ventral rami stay separate as the intercostal nerves.
At the neuromuscular junction acetylcholine acts on nicotinic receptors.

topics.title: Dermatomes and Myotomes
topics.summary: The areas of skin and the groups of muscles supplied by each spinal nerve.
points: A dermatome is the area of skin supplied by one spinal nerve; a myotome is the muscle supplied by one.
Key dermatomes: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 medial leg, L5 top of the foot, S1 lateral foot.
Key myotomes: C5 shoulder abduction, C6 elbow flexion, C7 elbow extension, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion, L5 big toe extension, S1 ankle plantarflexion.
Shingles (herpes zoster) produces a painful rash in one dermatome.

topics.title: Biomechanics and Kinesiology
topics.summary: Mechanics applied to the body: forces, levers, moments, stress and strain.
points: Forces through a joint can be several times body weight, because muscles act on short lever arms.
Bone adapts its structure to the loads placed on it (Wolff’s law).
The walking cycle has a stance phase (about 60%) and a swing phase (about 40%).
Analysis of movement guides training, rehabilitation and the design of implants.

topics.title: Prenatal Development
topics.summary: Development from fertilisation to birth.
points: Weeks 1 to 2: fertilisation, cleavage and implantation; weeks 3 to 8: the embryonic period, when the organs form; week 9 to birth: the fetal period of growth and maturation.
Gestational age is counted from the first day of the last menstrual period, about two weeks before fertilisation; term is 37 to 42 weeks.
The embryonic period is the time of greatest sensitivity to teratogens.
Folding in week 4 turns the flat embryo into a curved cylinder, enclosing the gut and forming the body cavities.

topics.title: Postnatal Growth and Maturation
topics.summary: How the body grows and matures from birth to adulthood.
points: Growth is fastest in infancy and again during the pubertal growth spurt.
Body proportions change: the head is about a quarter of body length at birth and about an eighth in adults.
Skeletal maturity (bone age) is judged from the ossification centres on a radiograph of the hand and wrist.
The growth plates fuse after puberty, ending growth in height.

topics.title: Ageing and Senescence Changes
topics.summary: The structural changes of ageing and their causes.
points: Cells accumulate damage, and telomeres shorten with repeated division.
Bone and muscle mass fall, and skin, lungs and arteries lose elasticity.
The brain loses volume and nerve conduction slows.
Kidney function declines with age, which affects the doses of many drugs.

topics.title: Molecular Embryology
topics.summary: The signals and genes that control how the embryo forms.
points: Key signalling molecules include Sonic hedgehog, Wnt, the BMP/TGF-β family, FGFs and retinoic acid.
HOX genes give each level of the head-to-tail axis its identity.
Induction is one tissue changing the fate of another, as when the notochord induces the neural plate.
Faults in these pathways cause malformations, such as holoprosencephaly with defects in Sonic hedgehog signalling.

topics.title: Stem Cell Differentiation
topics.summary: How unspecialised cells give rise to the specialised cells of the body.
points: The zygote is totipotent; cells of the inner cell mass are pluripotent; adult stem cells, such as haematopoietic stem cells, are multipotent.
Induced pluripotent stem cells are adult cells reprogrammed with a few transcription factors (Yamanaka, 2006).
Adult stem cells maintain tissues: in the bone marrow, at the base of the intestinal crypts and in the basal layer of the epidermis.
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation treats some blood cancers and bone marrow failure.

topics.title: Tissue Regeneration
topics.summary: How tissues repair themselves after injury, and why some cannot.
points: Labile tissues, such as the epidermis and the gut lining, renew constantly; stable tissues, such as the liver and kidney tubules, regenerate when injured; permanent tissues, such as neurons and cardiac muscle, barely regenerate.
The liver can regrow to its original size after part of it is removed.
When regeneration fails, lost tissue is replaced by a fibrous scar.
Peripheral nerves can regrow along their sheaths; axons in the brain and spinal cord largely cannot.

topics.title: Developmental Genetics
topics.summary: The genes that control development and the disorders caused when they go wrong.
points: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is associated with heart defects, duodenal atresia and characteristic facial features.
A mutation in FGFR3 causes achondroplasia; mutations in TBX5 cause Holt–Oram syndrome, affecting the heart and upper limbs.
One gene can affect several organs (pleiotropy).
The timing and dosage of gene activity are as important as the genes themselves.

topics.title: Epigenetics in Development
topics.summary: Changes in gene activity that do not alter the DNA sequence.
points: The main mechanisms are DNA methylation, histone modification and non-coding RNAs.
In genomic imprinting, some genes are active only on the copy from one parent; Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes arise this way.
X-inactivation silences one X chromosome in each cell of a female.
The environment in the womb, such as maternal nutrition, can alter epigenetic marks with long-term effects.

topics.title: Neuroembryology
topics.summary: How the nervous system develops.
points: The neural plate folds into the neural tube in week 4; the cranial opening closes at about day 25 and the caudal opening at about day 28.
Three primary brain vesicles (forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain) become five: telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon and myelencephalon.
The neural crest forms the sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes and the adrenal medulla.
Folic acid taken before conception and in early pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida.

topics.title: Cytoarchitecture of the Cerebral Cortex
topics.summary: The arrangement of cells in the layers and areas of the cerebral cortex.
points: The neocortex has six layers: molecular, external granular, external pyramidal, internal granular, internal pyramidal and multiform.
Brodmann mapped the cortex into numbered areas: 4 primary motor, 3-1-2 primary somatosensory, 17 primary visual, 41 primary auditory, 44 and 45 Broca’s area.
Motor cortex has a thick layer V with giant pyramidal (Betz) cells and almost no layer IV; sensory cortex has a thick layer IV.
The older allocortex, such as the hippocampus, has only three layers.

topics.title: White Matter Tracts
topics.summary: The bundles of myelinated axons that connect areas of the brain.
points: Association fibres join areas in the same hemisphere; the arcuate fasciculus links the language areas.
Commissural fibres cross between the hemispheres, mainly in the corpus callosum and anterior commissure.
Projection fibres join the cortex to lower centres through the corona radiata and internal capsule.
Diffusion tensor imaging maps these tracts in the living brain.

topics.title: Neurovascular Territory Mapping
topics.summary: Which arteries supply which parts of the brain, and how a stroke’s signs reveal the artery involved.
points: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg areas of the motor and sensory cortex.
The middle cerebral artery supplies most of the lateral surface, including the face and arm areas and, in the dominant hemisphere, the language areas.
The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe, including the visual cortex, and the inferior temporal lobe.
Weakness of the leg more than the arm suggests an anterior cerebral artery stroke; face and arm weakness with aphasia suggests the middle cerebral artery.

topics.title: Autonomic Reflex Arcs
topics.summary: Reflexes in which a sensory signal produces an automatic, autonomic response.
points: Visceral sensory fibres carry the signal to the spinal cord or brainstem, which sends autonomic output to the organ.
In the baroreceptor reflex, stretch of the carotid sinus and aortic arch (signalled by IX and X) slows the heart and widens vessels when blood pressure rises.
In the micturition reflex, bladder stretch acts through the sacral cord (S2 to S4) and the pontine micturition centre to contract the detrusor.
In the pupillary light reflex, light in one eye constricts both pupils through the pretectal and Edinger–Westphal nuclei and the oculomotor nerves.

topics.title: Neuroendocrine Pathways
topics.summary: The pathways through which the brain controls hormone release.
points: Hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol, the stress response.
Hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis: TRH, then TSH, then thyroid hormones.
Hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis: GnRH, then LH and FSH, then the sex steroids.
Sympathetic preganglionic fibres stimulate the adrenal medulla to release adrenaline.

topics.title: Functional Neuroimaging Correlation
topics.summary: Linking brain activity seen on imaging to anatomy and function.
points: Functional MRI detects changes in blood oxygenation (the BOLD signal) that follow neural activity.
PET measures glucose metabolism or the binding of tracers to receptors.
Finger tapping activates the opposite motor cortex; speaking activates Broca’s area.
It helps plan surgery near areas essential for movement and language.

topics.title: Fluoroscopy
topics.summary: Continuous X-ray imaging displayed as a moving picture.
points: It guides catheters, needles and fracture fixation and shows swallowing and other movements.
Contrast agents outline the gut, vessels and other hollow structures.
Radiation dose builds with screening time, so time is kept short, distance increased and shielding used.
It allows procedures to be watched as they happen.

topics.title: Positron Emission Tomography
topics.summary: Imaging that shows metabolic activity using a positron-emitting tracer (PET).
points: When a positron meets an electron, two gamma photons fly off in opposite directions and are detected.
The usual tracer, fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), is taken up by tissues that use a lot of glucose, such as many cancers, the brain and the heart.
It is combined with CT (PET-CT) to place activity on the anatomy.
It is used to stage cancers and judge their response to treatment, and in dementia and epilepsy.

topics.title: Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography
topics.summary: Three-dimensional imaging of a gamma-emitting tracer (SPECT).
points: A gamma camera rotates around the patient and detects single photons, usually from technetium-99m.
It shows function: heart muscle perfusion, brain blood flow, bone turnover and overactive parathyroid glands.
Its resolution is lower than CT, so it is often combined with CT (SPECT-CT).
The dose and choice of tracer depend on the organ studied.

topics.title: Doppler Ultrasonography
topics.summary: Ultrasound that measures blood flow from the change in frequency of sound reflected by moving blood.
points: Colour Doppler shows the direction of flow; spectral Doppler plots velocity over time.
It is used to find deep vein thrombosis, to grade carotid stenosis and to assess fetal and umbilical blood flow and heart valves.
Blood speeds up through a narrowing, so velocity is used to grade the severity of a stenosis.
It uses no ionising radiation.

topics.title: Endoscopic Ultrasonography
topics.summary: Ultrasound from a probe on the tip of an endoscope, scanning from inside the gut.
points: It shows the layers of the gut wall and nearby organs such as the pancreas, bile duct and lymph nodes in fine detail.
It stages oesophageal, gastric, pancreatic and rectal cancers by how deeply they invade.
It guides fine-needle aspiration and biopsy.
It can drain fluid collections next to the gut.

topics.title: Contrast Radiography
topics.summary: X-ray imaging made with a contrast agent to outline hollow organs or vessels.
points: Barium outlines the gut in swallows, meals, follow-through studies and enemas.
Iodinated contrast outlines vessels (angiography) and the urinary tract.
Iodinated contrast can cause allergic reactions and kidney injury, so risks are checked first.
If a perforation is suspected, water-soluble contrast is used instead of barium.

topics.title: Mammography
topics.summary: Low-dose X-ray imaging of the breast.
points: The breast is compressed between two plates to spread the tissue and reduce the dose.
The standard views are craniocaudal and mediolateral oblique.
It detects masses, distortion of the breast architecture and microcalcifications.
In the UK, the NHS screening programme invites women aged 50 to 71 every three years.

topics.title: Gross Anatomy
topics.summary: The study of structures visible to the naked eye.
points: It is learned through dissection, prosections, models, surface anatomy and imaging.
It can be studied region by region (regional anatomy) or system by system (systemic anatomy).
It is the foundation of clinical examination, imaging and surgery.
It includes the normal variation between people.

topics.title: Microscopic Anatomy
topics.summary: The study of structures visible only with a microscope: cells and tissues.
points: It includes cytology (cells) and histology (tissues).
Light microscopy resolves details down to about 0.2 micrometres; electron microscopy much finer.
It shows how structure serves function, as villi and microvilli enlarge the absorbing surface of the gut.
It is the basis of histopathology and diagnosis from tissue.

topics.title: Developmental Anatomy
topics.summary: The study of the body’s changes from conception to adulthood.
points: It includes embryology, fetal development and growth after birth.
It explains adult anatomy, such as why the testis drains to the para-aortic lymph nodes.
It explains congenital anomalies.
It covers growth, puberty and maturation.

topics.title: Embryology
topics.summary: The study of the embryo: development from fertilisation to the end of week 8, often extended to birth.
points: Key events are gastrulation, neurulation, folding and organogenesis.
Ectoderm forms the skin and nervous system; mesoderm the muscles, bones, heart, blood and kidneys; endoderm the lining of the gut and airways, the liver and the pancreas.
Weeks 3 to 8 are the critical period for major malformations.
It explains many adult relations and congenital anomalies.

topics.title: Histology
topics.summary: The study of tissues with the microscope.
points: All organs are built from four basic tissues: epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.
Routine sections are stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E).
Special stains and immunohistochemistry show particular substances and cells.
Histopathology diagnoses disease from tissue samples.

topics.title: Cytology
topics.summary: The study of cells: their structure, organelles and function.
points: Each cell is bounded by a phospholipid bilayer membrane and contains a nucleus and organelles.
Cells divide by mitosis to grow and renew tissues, and by meiosis to make gametes.
Diagnostic cytology examines loose cells from fluids, scrapes or fine-needle aspiration, as in cervical screening.
Changes in nuclear size and shape can signal malignancy.

topics.title: Neuroanatomy
topics.summary: The study of the structure of the nervous system.
points: It covers the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (12 pairs of cranial and 31 pairs of spinal nerves).
Grey matter is mainly neuron cell bodies; white matter is mainly myelinated axons.
Knowledge of pathways lets clinicians locate a lesion from the signs.
It underpins neurology, neurosurgery and neuroradiology.

topics.title: Surface Anatomy
topics.summary: The study of deep structures through the features of the body’s surface.
points: Key landmarks include the sternal angle, the xiphoid process, the umbilicus (around the L3–L4 disc) and the iliac crests (L4).
It guides examination, injections, cannulation and the placing of the stethoscope.
Heart sounds are heard best at: aortic, right second intercostal space; pulmonary, left second space; tricuspid, lower left sternal edge; mitral, the apex.
Landmarks shift with age, posture and body build.

topics.title: Regional Anatomy
topics.summary: Studying the body region by region: back, upper limb, thorax, abdomen, pelvis and perineum, lower limb, head and neck.
points: It shows every system in a region together, with their relations.
It matches how clinicians examine and how surgeons operate.
It is usually taught alongside dissection.
It complements systemic anatomy.

topics.title: Systemic Anatomy
topics.summary: Studying the body one organ system at a time.
points: It shows how the parts of a system work together for one function.
It matches medical specialties such as cardiology or neurology.
It is useful for understanding physiology and disease.
It complements regional anatomy.

topics.title: Sectional Anatomy
topics.summary: The study of the body in sections: axial, coronal and sagittal.
points: It is the basis for reading CT and MRI.
It is taught with frozen or plastinated sections alongside scans.
It demands a three-dimensional understanding of relations.
Standard levels, such as the transpyloric plane, help orientation.

topics.title: Radiological Anatomy
topics.summary: Anatomy as shown by medical imaging.
points: Plain radiographs, CT, MRI, ultrasound and angiography each show tissues differently: bone is white on radiographs; fluid is bright on T2-weighted MRI.
Normal variants must be recognised so they are not mistaken for disease.
A systematic way of reviewing every image avoids missed findings.
It links the dissecting room with clinical practice.

topics.title: Clinical Anatomy
topics.summary: Anatomy applied to the diagnosis and treatment of patients.
points: It explains signs and symptoms, such as referred pain and the patterns of nerve injury.
It guides procedures: injections, cannulation, drains and nerve blocks.
It is often taught through clinical cases.
It connects anatomy to examination, imaging and surgery.

topics.title: Applied Anatomy
topics.summary: Anatomy put to practical use in medicine, surgery, sport and ergonomics.
points: Examples include choosing safe injection sites, placing nerve blocks and designing splints.
It focuses on function and on the effects of injury.
It overlaps closely with clinical anatomy.
It turns knowledge of structure into safe practice.

topics.title: Surgical Anatomy
topics.summary: The anatomy needed to operate safely: planes, vessels, nerves and their variations.
points: It identifies the structures at risk, such as the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroidectomy and the common bile duct in cholecystectomy.
It includes incisions, approaches and surgical planes.
Unrecognised variations, such as unusual arterial origins, cause complications.
It is learned from dissection, imaging and the operating theatre.

topics.title: Comparative Anatomy
topics.summary: Comparing the structure of different species.
points: Homologous structures share an origin, as the forelimbs of vertebrates do; analogous structures share a function but not an origin, as bird and insect wings do.
It provides evidence for evolution.
Animal models in research depend on understanding how they differ from humans.
It explains vestigial and variant structures in humans.

topics.title: Functional Anatomy
topics.summary: Relating structure to function: how muscles move joints and how organs do their work.
points: A muscle’s action depends on its line of pull relative to the joint’s axis.
Alveoli give a huge, thin surface for gas exchange; villi and microvilli enlarge the gut’s absorbing surface.
It underpins physiotherapy, sport science and rehabilitation.
It explains the effects of injury on movement.

topics.title: Pathological Anatomy
topics.summary: The study of the structural changes caused by disease (morbid anatomy).
points: It includes gross changes seen at surgery and autopsy and microscopic changes seen in histopathology.
Giovanni Battista Morgagni linked symptoms in life to findings at autopsy in 1761.
Autopsy confirms the cause of death and audits diagnosis.
It forms the basis of modern pathology.

topics.title: Osteology
topics.summary: The study of bones.
points: The adult skeleton has 206 bones, which may be long, short, flat, irregular or sesamoid.
Compact bone forms the outer shell; spongy (trabecular) bone inside holds red marrow.
Processes, tubercles, foramina and fossae mark attachments and passages.
Bones store calcium and phosphate and make blood cells.

topics.title: Arthrology
topics.summary: The study of joints.
points: Joints are classified as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial.
A synovial joint has articular cartilage, a fibrous capsule lined by synovial membrane, and synovial fluid.
Each joint has a characteristic range of movement.
Osteoarthritis wears away cartilage; rheumatoid arthritis inflames the synovial membrane.

topics.title: Myology
topics.summary: The study of muscles.
points: There are three types: skeletal, cardiac and smooth.
The body has more than 600 skeletal muscles.
Names describe shape, size, position, number of heads, action or attachments.
Parallel fibres favour range and speed; pennate fibres favour force.

topics.title: Angiology
topics.summary: The study of blood and lymphatic vessels.
points: Vessel walls have three layers: tunica intima, tunica media and tunica adventitia.
Arteries have a thicker media; veins have a wider lumen and, in the limbs, valves.
Capillaries are a single layer of endothelium for exchange.
Atherosclerosis narrows arteries and causes heart attack, stroke and limb ischaemia.

topics.title: Neurology
topics.summary: In anatomy, the study of the structure of the nervous system; in medicine, the specialty of its diseases.
points: It covers the central and peripheral nervous systems, with their somatic and autonomic parts.
The neurological examination tests anatomy: cranial nerves, power, tone, reflexes, sensation and coordination.
Localising a lesion depends on knowing the pathways.
Imaging confirms the site suggested by the examination.

topics.title: Splanchnology
topics.summary: The study of the viscera: the internal organs of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.
points: It covers the digestive, respiratory, urinary and reproductive organs.
Organs are hollow (tubular) or solid (parenchymatous).
Visceral pain is poorly localised and often referred to the body wall.
Their relation to the serous membranes decides whether they are intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal.

topics.title: Endocrinology
topics.summary: In anatomy, the study of the endocrine glands; in medicine, the specialty of hormone disorders.
points: Ductless glands release hormones into the blood: pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreatic islets and gonads.
They have a rich blood supply with fenestrated capillaries.
Hormones act on target cells through receptors and are controlled by feedback.
Disorders result from too much or too little hormone.

topics.title: Dermatology
topics.summary: In anatomy, the study of the skin; in medicine, the specialty of skin disease.
points: The epidermis is keratinised stratified squamous epithelium in layers: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum (in thick skin) and corneum.
Below lie the dermis and the subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis).
Appendages include hair, nails, eccrine and apocrine sweat glands and sebaceous glands.
The skin protects, regulates temperature, senses touch and makes vitamin D.

topics.title: Organology
topics.summary: The study of the organs.
points: Organs consist of parenchyma (working cells) and stroma (supporting tissue).
Each has its own blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply.
Organs are grouped by system and by region.
Organ transplantation depends on detailed knowledge of organ anatomy.

topics.title: Anatomical Terminology
topics.summary: The precise vocabulary of anatomy.
points: It is built largely from Latin and Greek roots: cardi- (heart), hepat- (liver), -itis (inflammation), -ectomy (removal).
The international standard is Terminologia Anatomica.
Terms describe position, shape, size or function.
Precise terms such as “anterior” avoid confusion whatever the patient’s position.

topics.title: Anatomical Position
topics.summary: The standard reference position for describing the body.
points: The body stands upright, facing forwards, with the arms at the sides, the palms facing forwards and the feet together.
All descriptions refer to this position, whatever position the patient is actually in.
Supine means lying face up; prone means lying face down.
Right and left always mean the patient’s right and left.

topics.title: Anatomical Planes and Axes
topics.summary: The imaginary flat surfaces and lines used to describe sections and movements.
points: The median plane divides the body into right and left halves; other sagittal planes run parallel to it.
Coronal (frontal) planes divide front from back; transverse (axial) planes divide upper from lower.
Flexion and extension happen in the sagittal plane, abduction and adduction in the coronal plane and rotation in the transverse plane.
Each movement turns around an axis at right angles to its plane.

topics.title: Terms of Location and Direction
topics.summary: The words that describe where structures lie relative to each other.
points: Superior and inferior (or cranial and caudal), anterior and posterior (or ventral and dorsal), medial and lateral.
Proximal and distal describe the limbs; superficial and deep describe depth.
Ipsilateral means the same side; contralateral the opposite side.
The hand has palmar and dorsal surfaces; the foot has plantar and dorsal surfaces.

topics.title: Terms of Movement
topics.summary: The words that describe how body parts move at joints.
points: Flexion decreases the angle of a joint; extension increases it.
Abduction moves a part away from the midline; adduction moves it towards the midline.
Medial and lateral rotation turn a part around its long axis; circumduction combines movements in a circle.
Special terms include pronation and supination, inversion and eversion, dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, protraction and retraction, elevation and depression, and opposition.

topics.title: Anatomical Variations
topics.summary: The normal differences in anatomy between individuals.
points: Palmaris longus is absent in roughly 15% of people.
The brachial artery may divide high in the arm, and extra renal arteries are common.
Variations matter in surgery, procedures and the reading of scans.
They differ from anomalies, which may cause disease.

topics.title: Integumentary System
topics.summary: The skin and its appendages: hair, nails and glands.
points: The skin has an outer epidermis and an inner dermis, over the subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis).
It protects against water loss, microbes and ultraviolet light, and makes vitamin D.
It controls temperature through sweating and skin blood flow, and senses touch through receptors such as Meissner’s corpuscles (light touch) and Pacinian corpuscles (vibration and pressure).
Burns are graded by depth: superficial (epidermis), partial thickness (into the dermis) and full thickness (the whole dermis, often painless and needing grafts).

topics.title: Skeletal System
topics.summary: The bones and the cartilage that support and protect the body and make movement possible.
points: The adult skeleton has 206 bones: 80 in the axial skeleton and 126 in the appendicular skeleton.
It supports, protects, provides levers for movement, stores minerals and makes blood cells.
In adults, red marrow is found mainly in the flat bones and the ends of long bones, such as the sternum, vertebrae and pelvis.
Bone mass peaks at around 30 years of age and then slowly declines.

topics.title: Articular System
topics.summary: The joints and the ligaments that hold them together.
points: Joints are classified as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial.
Synovial joints are the most mobile; their stability comes from bone shape, ligaments and muscles.
Bursae and tendon sheaths reduce friction where tendons pass close to bone.
Each joint’s shape determines its range and types of movement.

topics.title: Muscular System
topics.summary: The skeletal muscles that move the body, maintain posture and produce heat.
points: Skeletal muscle is striated and under voluntary control; cardiac and smooth muscle are found in the heart and in hollow organs.
Each muscle pulls on bones through its tendons, from an origin to an insertion.
Muscle contracts as actin and myosin filaments slide past each other, triggered by calcium (sliding filament theory).
A motor unit is one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies.

topics.title: Nervous System
topics.summary: The network that senses, integrates and controls the body’s activities.
points: It has a central part (brain and spinal cord) and a peripheral part (cranial and spinal nerves and their ganglia).
Functionally it has somatic and autonomic divisions, each with sensory and motor parts.
It is built of neurons and supporting glial cells.
Signals travel along neurons as action potentials and cross synapses chemically.

topics.title: Central Nervous System
topics.summary: The brain and the spinal cord.
points: The brain consists of the cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum.
Bone, the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid protect it.
In the cerebrum the grey matter is on the outside (the cortex); in the spinal cord it is on the inside.
Myelin in the CNS is made by oligodendrocytes; multiple sclerosis damages it.

topics.title: Peripheral Nervous System
topics.summary: The nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord.
points: It includes 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.
Each spinal nerve forms from a dorsal (sensory) and a ventral (motor) root and carries both kinds of fibre.
Myelin in the PNS is made by Schwann cells, and damaged peripheral nerves can regenerate.
Peripheral neuropathy, such as diabetic neuropathy, often begins in the feet and hands (“glove and stocking”).

topics.title: Autonomic Nervous System
topics.summary: The part of the nervous system that controls involuntary functions: the heart, smooth muscle and glands.
points: The sympathetic division prepares the body for action: it speeds the heart, widens the pupils and airways and diverts blood to the muscles.
The parasympathetic division supports rest and digestion: it slows the heart, narrows the pupils and promotes digestion.
The vagus nerve carries most of the parasympathetic outflow.
The enteric nervous system of the gut is sometimes counted as a third division.

topics.title: Cardiovascular System
topics.summary: The heart and blood vessels, which carry blood around the body.
points: The heart has four chambers and four valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral and aortic).
Each beat begins in the sinoatrial node and spreads through the atrioventricular node, the bundle of His, the bundle branches and the Purkinje fibres.
The heart muscle is supplied by the right and left coronary arteries.
The pulmonary and systemic circulations work in series.

topics.title: Circulatory System
topics.summary: The circuits through which blood, and with it lymph, flows around the body.
points: Blood flows from arteries to arterioles, capillaries, venules and veins.
In a portal system blood passes through two capillary beds in turn, as in the hepatic portal system and the pituitary portal system.
An adult has about 5 litres of blood.
The lymphatic system returns fluid that leaks from the capillaries.

topics.title: Lymphatic System
topics.summary: Lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes and lymphoid organs.
points: It returns several litres of tissue fluid to the blood each day.
Lymphatic vessels in the gut (lacteals) absorb dietary fat as chyle.
Lymph nodes filter lymph and are where immune responses begin.
Enlarged lymph nodes may signal infection or cancer.

topics.title: Respiratory System
topics.summary: The airways and lungs, which bring air into contact with blood for gas exchange.
points: The conducting zone runs from the nose to the terminal bronchioles; the respiratory zone includes the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli.
Hundreds of millions of alveoli give a gas-exchange surface of roughly 70 square metres.
Breathing in is driven by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles; quiet breathing out is passive.
The upper airway warms, moistens and filters the air, and the mucociliary escalator clears particles.

topics.title: Digestive System
topics.summary: The gastrointestinal tract and the accessory organs: salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas.
points: It takes in food, breaks it down mechanically and chemically, absorbs nutrients and eliminates waste.
Waves of muscle contraction (peristalsis) move the contents along.
Blood from the gut passes through the liver in the hepatic portal vein before reaching the general circulation (first-pass metabolism).
The pancreas adds digestive enzymes and the liver adds bile, which emulsifies fat.

topics.title: Urinary System
topics.summary: The kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra.
points: The kidneys filter about 180 litres of plasma a day and produce about 1.5 litres of urine.
They regulate water, salts, acid–base balance and blood pressure (through renin).
They also make erythropoietin and activate vitamin D.
The bladder stores urine; its usual capacity is about 400 to 600 mL.

topics.title: Urogenital System
topics.summary: The urinary and reproductive organs, studied together because they develop together.
points: Both arise from the intermediate mesoderm and the cloaca.
In males the urethra carries both urine and semen.
The organs lie close together; the prostate, for example, surrounds the urethra.
Congenital anomalies often affect both systems.

topics.title: Male Reproductive System
topics.summary: The organs that produce, store and deliver sperm and make testosterone.
points: The testes make sperm and testosterone; sperm mature in the epididymis.
Sperm travel through the ductus (vas) deferens and ejaculatory duct into the urethra in the prostate.
The seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands add the fluid of semen.
The scrotum keeps the testes about 2 to 3 °C below core body temperature, which sperm production needs.

topics.title: Female Reproductive System
topics.summary: The ovaries, uterine tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina and external genitalia.
points: The ovaries produce oocytes and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone.
Fertilisation usually takes place in the ampulla of the uterine tube.
The menstrual cycle has ovarian phases (follicular, ovulation, luteal) and uterine phases (menstrual, proliferative, secretory).
The uterus supports the developing pregnancy.

topics.title: Endocrine System
topics.summary: The glands and cells that release hormones into the blood.
points: The main glands are the hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreatic islets and gonads.
The heart, kidneys, gut and fat also produce hormones.
Most hormone levels are controlled by negative feedback.
Thyroid hormones set the metabolic rate; parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium.

topics.title: Immune System
topics.summary: The cells, tissues and organs that defend the body against infection.
points: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific: barriers, neutrophils, macrophages, natural killer cells and complement.
Adaptive immunity is specific and has memory: B cells make antibodies; helper (CD4) and cytotoxic (CD8) T cells coordinate and kill.
The bone marrow and thymus are primary lymphoid organs; lymph nodes, spleen and mucosal lymphoid tissue are secondary.
Vaccination uses immunological memory to protect against infection.

topics.title: Special Senses
topics.summary: Vision, hearing, balance, smell and taste.
points: Each has specialised receptor cells that turn a stimulus into nerve signals.
The retina holds rods and cones; the cochlea and vestibular apparatus hold hair cells.
The olfactory epithelium detects smells and the taste buds detect taste.
They are carried by cranial nerves I, II, VII, VIII, IX and X.

topics.title: Back
topics.summary: The posterior part of the trunk, built around the vertebral column.
points: The vertebral column has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae, the sacrum (5 fused vertebrae) and the coccyx.
The cervical and lumbar regions curve forwards (lordosis); the thoracic and sacral regions curve backwards (kyphosis).
The deep muscles of the back, such as erector spinae, extend the spine and are supplied by the dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.
A disc’s nucleus pulposus can herniate through its annulus fibrosus, usually posterolaterally, compressing a nerve root: an L4–L5 disc usually affects the L5 root.

topics.title: Upper Limb
topics.summary: The shoulder, arm, elbow, forearm, wrist and hand: built for reach and fine movement.
points: The brachial plexus (C5 to T1) has roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches.
Its five terminal branches are the musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves.
The subclavian artery becomes the axillary and then the brachial artery, which divides into the radial and ulnar arteries.
The shoulder girdle links the limb to the trunk only at the sternoclavicular joint.

topics.title: Lower Limb
topics.summary: The gluteal region, thigh, knee, leg, ankle and foot: built to bear weight and move the body.
points: The lumbar (L1 to L4) and sacral (L4 to S4) plexuses give the femoral, obturator and sciatic nerves.
The external iliac artery becomes the femoral and then the popliteal artery, which divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
Calf muscle contraction and venous valves push blood back to the heart; immobility raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis.
The arches of the foot spread the load of the body.

topics.title: Thorax
topics.summary: The chest: the thoracic cage and the organs within it.
points: The thoracic cage protects the heart, lungs and great vessels.
The lungs lie in the pleural cavities on each side of the mediastinum, which holds the heart.
The diaphragm separates the thorax from the abdomen.
Breathing in enlarges the thorax in all three dimensions.

topics.title: Abdomen
topics.summary: The region between the diaphragm and the pelvic inlet.
points: It is divided into four quadrants or nine regions to describe pain and findings.
It contains most of the digestive tract, the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, adrenal glands and great vessels.
Many organs are covered by peritoneum; others lie behind it.
The muscular abdominal wall protects the organs and moves the trunk.

topics.title: Pelvis
topics.summary: The bony basin at the base of the trunk and the organs within it.
points: The bony pelvis is formed by the two hip bones (each made of ilium, ischium and pubis), the sacrum and the coccyx.
The pelvic brim divides the greater (false) pelvis above from the lesser (true) pelvis below.
It contains the bladder, rectum and internal reproductive organs.
The pelvic floor closes it below and supports the organs.

topics.title: Perineum
topics.summary: The diamond-shaped region below the pelvic floor, between the thighs.
points: It runs from the pubic symphysis in front to the coccyx behind.
A line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into the urogenital triangle in front and the anal triangle behind.
It is supplied by the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) and the internal pudendal vessels.
The perineal body, its central tendinous point, is important in childbirth.

topics.title: Head
topics.summary: The skull and its contents: the brain, the special sense organs and the start of the airway and digestive tract.
points: The skull has 8 cranial bones around the brain and 14 facial bones.
It houses the organs of vision, hearing, balance, smell and taste.
Twelve pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain.
The internal and external carotid arteries and the vertebral arteries supply it.

topics.title: Neck
topics.summary: The region that joins the head to the trunk.
points: It is supported by the seven cervical vertebrae.
Fascial layers include the investing, pretracheal and prevertebral layers and the carotid sheath.
It contains the larynx, trachea, pharynx, oesophagus, thyroid and parathyroid glands, great vessels, cranial nerves IX to XII and the cervical and brachial plexuses.
It is divided into triangles for examination.

topics.title: Cell Biology
topics.summary: The structure and function of cells, the basic units of life.
points: The plasma membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.
The nucleus holds the DNA; mitochondria make ATP; ribosomes make proteins, which the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus process.
The cytoskeleton of microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules gives shape and movement.
The cell cycle (G1, S, G2 and M phases) has checkpoints that stop damaged cells from dividing.

topics.title: Epithelial Tissue
topics.summary: The tissue that covers surfaces and lines cavities and forms glands.
points: It sits on a basement membrane and has no blood vessels of its own.
It is classified by its number of layers (simple, stratified or pseudostratified) and its cell shape (squamous, cuboidal or columnar).

Examples: simple squamous in the alveoli and vessels, simple columnar in the gut, stratified squamous in the skin and oesophagus, transitional (urothelium) in the bladder and pseudostratified ciliated columnar in the airways.
Glands are exocrine (secreting through ducts) or endocrine (secreting into the blood).

topics.title: Connective Tissue
topics.summary: The tissue that supports, binds and protects other tissues.
points: It consists of cells, such as fibroblasts, in an extracellular matrix of fibres and ground substance.
Collagen fibres give strength, elastic fibres stretch and recoil, and reticular fibres form fine supporting networks.
Types include loose, dense regular (tendons and ligaments), dense irregular (dermis) and adipose tissue; cartilage, bone and blood are specialised connective tissues.
All connective tissues come from embryonic mesenchyme.

topics.title: Cartilage
topics.summary: A firm, flexible connective tissue made by chondrocytes.
points: Chondrocytes lie in spaces (lacunae) in the matrix; cartilage has no blood vessels and is fed by diffusion, so it heals poorly.
Hyaline cartilage covers joint surfaces and forms the costal cartilages and the rings of the trachea.
Elastic cartilage forms the auricle and epiglottis; fibrocartilage forms the intervertebral discs, menisci and pubic symphysis.
Most cartilage is covered by perichondrium, but articular cartilage is not.

topics.title: Bone Tissue
topics.summary: The hard, mineralised connective tissue of the skeleton.
points: Its cells are osteoblasts (which build bone), osteocytes (which maintain it) and osteoclasts (which resorb it).
The matrix is type I collagen hardened by hydroxyapatite crystals.
Compact bone is made of osteons (Haversian systems) around central canals; spongy bone is made of trabeculae.
Woven bone forms first in development and fracture healing and is replaced by lamellar bone.

topics.title: Muscle Tissue
topics.summary: The tissue specialised for contraction.
points: Skeletal muscle fibres are long, striated and multinucleated, under voluntary control.
Cardiac muscle cells are striated and branched, with central nuclei, joined by intercalated discs with gap junctions.
Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped without striations and line hollow organs and vessels.
In striated muscle the sarcomere, from Z-disc to Z-disc, contains thin actin and thick myosin filaments.

topics.title: Nervous Tissue
topics.summary: The tissue of neurons and glial cells.
points: A neuron has a cell body, dendrites that receive signals and an axon that sends them; neurons may be multipolar, bipolar or pseudounipolar.
Glial cells support, insulate and protect neurons.
Myelin speeds conduction, with impulses jumping between the nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction).
At a synapse, neurotransmitter released by one neuron acts on receptors of the next.

topics.title: Blood and Haematopoiesis
topics.summary: The blood and the formation of its cells (haematopoiesis).
points: Blood is about 55% plasma and 45% cells: red cells, white cells and platelets.
All blood cells arise from haematopoietic stem cells in the red bone marrow.
Red cells live about 120 days and platelets about 7 to 10 days.
Erythropoietin from the kidney drives the production of red cells.

topics.title: Ultrastructure of Tissues
topics.summary: The fine structure of tissues seen with the electron microscope.
points: It shows cell junctions, the basement membrane, microvilli (the brush border) and cilia with their 9+2 arrangement of microtubules.
Organelles reflect function: plasma cells are packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum, kidney tubule cells with mitochondria.
The glomerular filtration barrier consists of fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane and the slit diaphragms between podocytes.
In muscle it shows the sarcomere and the T-tubules.

topics.title: Organ Microanatomy
topics.summary: The microscopic structure of the organs.
points: The liver is organised in lobules around central veins, with portal triads at their corners.
The lung’s alveoli are lined by thin type I pneumocytes and surfactant-making type II pneumocytes.
The gut wall changes along its length: gastric pits in the stomach, villi in the small intestine and crypts rich in goblet cells in the colon.
A lymph node has a cortex with follicles, a paracortex and a medulla.

topics.title: Gametogenesis
topics.summary: The formation of sperm and eggs by meiosis.
points: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, from 46 to 23.
Spermatogenesis runs continuously from puberty in the seminiferous tubules; each cycle takes about two months, and each primary spermatocyte gives four sperm.
Oogenesis begins before birth: primary oocytes pause in the first meiotic division until ovulation, and each gives one egg and polar bodies.
Errors in meiosis (non-disjunction) cause abnormal chromosome numbers and become more frequent with maternal age.

topics.title: Fertilisation
topics.summary: The union of a sperm and an egg to form a zygote (fertilisation).
points: It usually takes place in the ampulla of the uterine tube within about 24 hours of ovulation.
Sperm undergo capacitation and the acrosome reaction to pass through the zona pellucida.
The cortical reaction then blocks entry by other sperm.
The two pronuclei combine to form a diploid zygote; the sperm’s X or Y chromosome determines its genetic sex.

topics.title: Cleavage and Implantation
topics.summary: The early divisions of the zygote and its attachment to the wall of the uterus.
points: The zygote divides into a morula by about day 3 to 4 and a blastocyst, with an inner cell mass and trophoblast, by day 4 to 5.
The blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida and implants in the uterine wall at about day 6 to 7.
The syncytiotrophoblast invades the endometrium and secretes hCG, the hormone detected by pregnancy tests.
Implantation outside the uterus, most often in the uterine tube, is an ectopic pregnancy.

topics.title: Gastrulation
topics.summary: The process in week 3 that turns the two-layered embryonic disc into three germ layers.
points: The primitive streak forms; epiblast cells move through it to form the endoderm and mesoderm, and the remaining epiblast becomes the ectoderm.
The notochord forms in the midline and induces the neural plate.
The body axes (head–tail, front–back, left–right) are established.
Errors at this stage cause severe malformations.

topics.title: Neurulation
topics.summary: The formation of the neural tube, the forerunner of the brain and spinal cord.
points: The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate in week 3.
The neural folds rise and fuse into a tube, beginning in the future neck and closing towards both ends.
Neural crest cells leave the edges of the folds and migrate widely.
Failure to close causes anencephaly at the head end or spina bifida at the tail end.

topics.title: Organogenesis
topics.summary: The formation of the organs, mainly in weeks 3 to 8.
points: All the major organ systems begin to form in this period.
Head-to-tail and side-to-side folding shapes the body and incorporates part of the yolk sac to form the gut.
The heart is the first organ to function.
This is the period of greatest sensitivity to teratogens.

topics.title: Pharyngeal Arches
topics.summary: Paired arches in the neck of the embryo, each with its own cartilage, muscle, artery and nerve.
points: They appear in weeks 4 and 5; the fifth arch does not develop in humans.
First arch: the muscles of mastication, the malleus and incus, supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).
Second arch: the muscles of facial expression, the stapes and the styloid process, supplied by the facial nerve (VII).
Third arch: stylopharyngeus and part of the hyoid (IX); fourth and sixth arches: the laryngeal cartilages and muscles, supplied by the superior and recurrent laryngeal branches of the vagus.

topics.title: Placentation
topics.summary: The formation and functions of the placenta.
points: The placenta forms from the chorion frondosum (fetal) and the decidua basalis (maternal).
Maternal blood bathes the chorionic villi in the intervillous space; fetal and maternal blood do not normally mix.
It exchanges gases, nutrients and waste and makes hormones: hCG, progesterone, oestrogens and human placental lactogen.
IgG antibodies cross it, as do many drugs and some infections.

topics.title: Fetal Circulation
topics.summary: The circulation before birth, which bypasses the lungs and partly the liver.
points: Oxygenated blood from the placenta travels in the umbilical vein; the ductus venosus lets much of it bypass the liver.
The foramen ovale passes blood from the right to the left atrium, and the ductus arteriosus from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta.
Two umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.

After birth the foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis, the ductus arteriosus the ligamentum arteriosum, the ductus venosus the ligamentum venosum, the umbilical vein the ligamentum teres and the umbilical arteries the medial umbilical ligaments.

topics.title: Teratology
topics.summary: The study of the causes of congenital malformations.
points: Teratogens include drugs (such as thalidomide, isotretinoin, valproate and warfarin), alcohol, infections (such as rubella, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis and Zika), radiation and poorly controlled maternal diabetes.
The embryo is most sensitive in weeks 3 to 8, when the organs form; before that, exposure tends to cause either loss of the embryo or no effect.
The effect depends on the dose, timing and genetic susceptibility.
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is a leading preventable cause of learning disability.

topics.title: Congenital Malformations
topics.summary: Structural abnormalities present at birth.
points: About 2 to 3% of babies are born with a major malformation.
Causes are genetic, environmental or, most often, a mix of both (multifactorial).
Common examples include congenital heart defects, neural tube defects, cleft lip and palate, talipes and hypospadias.
Many are detected by antenatal screening.

topics.title: Neurohistology
topics.summary: The microscopic structure of the nervous system.
points: Neuron cell bodies contain Nissl bodies (rough endoplasmic reticulum).
Glial cells of the CNS are astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and ependymal cells; those of the PNS are Schwann cells and satellite cells.
Grey matter is rich in cell bodies; white matter is rich in myelinated axons.
A peripheral nerve is wrapped in endoneurium, perineurium and epineurium.

topics.title: Meninges and Cerebrospinal Fluid
topics.summary: The three membranes around the brain and spinal cord and the fluid between them.
points: From outside in: dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater.

An extradural haematoma (usually arterial, often from the middle meningeal artery) lies between skull and dura; a subdural haematoma (from bridging veins) between dura and arachnoid; a subarachnoid haemorrhage bleeds into the CSF.
Cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain and carries away waste.
Meningitis inflames the meninges, causing headache, neck stiffness and dislike of light.

topics.title: Ventricular System
topics.summary: The connected cavities within the brain that contain cerebrospinal fluid.
points: There are two lateral ventricles, a third ventricle and a fourth ventricle, joined by the interventricular foramina and the cerebral aqueduct.
They are lined by ependyma, and the choroid plexuses within them make CSF.
The fourth ventricle opens into the subarachnoid space through one median and two lateral apertures.
Narrowing of the cerebral aqueduct causes hydrocephalus of the lateral and third ventricles.

topics.title: Blood Supply of the Brain
topics.summary: The arteries and veins of the brain.
points: The brain is supplied by the two internal carotid arteries and the two vertebral arteries, which join to form the basilar artery.
The arterial circle at the base of the brain (circle of Willis) links the two systems.
The brain receives about 15% of the cardiac output.
Veins drain into the dural venous sinuses and then into the internal jugular veins.

topics.title: Spinal Cord
topics.summary: The part of the central nervous system in the vertebral canal.
points: It runs from the foramen magnum to about L1–L2 in adults, ending as the conus medullaris; the cauda equina continues below.
Cervical and lumbar enlargements supply the limbs.
Its grey matter has dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) horns, and lateral horns from T1 to L2 for sympathetic neurons.
Cauda equina syndrome, with saddle numbness and bladder or bowel dysfunction, is a surgical emergency.

topics.title: Brainstem
topics.summary: The midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata, joining the cerebrum to the spinal cord.
points: It holds the nuclei of cranial nerves III to XII.
All the long ascending and descending tracts pass through it.
It contains vital centres that control breathing and the circulation.
Brainstem reflexes are tested in the diagnosis of death by neurological criteria.

topics.title: Cerebellum
topics.summary: The part of the brain that coordinates movement, balance and posture.
points: It lies in the posterior cranial fossa and joins the brainstem through three pairs of cerebellar peduncles.
It compares intended with actual movement and helps motor learning.
Damage causes signs on the same side: ataxia, intention tremor, difficulty with rapid alternating movements, nystagmus and slurred speech.
Its cortex has three layers, and Purkinje cells provide its only output, to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

topics.title: Diencephalon
topics.summary: The central part of the forebrain: thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus and subthalamus.
points: The thalamus relays sensory and motor information to the cortex; smell is the only sense that does not pass through it first.
The hypothalamus controls temperature, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythms (through the suprachiasmatic nucleus) and the pituitary.
The pineal gland, in the epithalamus, secretes melatonin.
The subthalamic nucleus works with the basal ganglia.

topics.title: Cerebrum
topics.summary: The two cerebral hemispheres, the largest part of the brain.
points: Each hemisphere has frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes and the insula.
The cortex is folded into gyri and sulci; the central sulcus separates the motor cortex in front from the sensory cortex behind.
Language is usually based in the left hemisphere.
The motor and sensory cortex hold maps of the body (homunculi).

topics.title: Basal Ganglia
topics.summary: Deep nuclei that help select and regulate movement.
points: They include the caudate nucleus, putamen and globus pallidus, working with the subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra.
The caudate nucleus and putamen together form the striatum.
The direct pathway facilitates movement; the indirect pathway suppresses unwanted movement.
Disorders include Parkinson’s disease and Huntington’s disease.

topics.title: Limbic System
topics.summary: Brain structures involved in emotion, memory and behaviour.
points: It includes the hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, fornix and mammillary bodies, with parts of the thalamus.
The Papez circuit links the hippocampus, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus and cingulate gyrus.
The hippocampus is essential for forming new memories and is damaged early in Alzheimer’s disease.
The amygdala processes fear and emotional memory.

topics.title: Cranial Nerves
topics.summary: The twelve pairs of nerves that arise from the brain.
points: I olfactory, II optic, III oculomotor, IV trochlear, V trigeminal, VI abducens, VII facial, VIII vestibulocochlear, IX glossopharyngeal, X vagus, XI accessory and XII hypoglossal.
I, II and VIII are sensory; III, IV, VI, XI and XII are motor; V, VII, IX and X are mixed.
Parasympathetic fibres travel in III, VII, IX and X.
Each is tested in the neurological examination.

topics.title: Spinal Nerves
topics.summary: The 31 pairs of nerves that leave the spinal cord.
points: There are 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal pair.
C1 to C7 leave above the vertebra of the same number; C8 leaves below C7, and every nerve below that leaves below its own vertebra.
Each divides into a dorsal ramus (to the back) and a ventral ramus (to the limbs and the front of the trunk).
A posterolateral disc herniation at L4–L5 usually compresses the L5 nerve root.

topics.title: Ascending and Descending Tracts
topics.summary: The long pathways of the spinal cord and brainstem.
points: Ascending tracts: the dorsal columns (fine touch and proprioception), spinothalamic tracts (pain and temperature) and spinocerebellar tracts (unconscious proprioception).
Descending tracts: the corticospinal tract (voluntary movement), with the reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, rubrospinal and tectospinal tracts.
The level at which each tract crosses decides on which side the signs of a lesion appear.
Cord lesions give recognisable patterns, such as the Brown-Séquard syndrome.

topics.title: Visual Pathway
topics.summary: The route from the retina to the visual cortex.
points: Retina, optic nerve, optic chiasm (where the fibres from the nasal halves of the retinas cross), optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiation and the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
A lesion of one optic nerve blinds that eye; a lesion of the chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopia; lesions behind the chiasm cause a homonymous hemianopia on the opposite side.
Fibres of the optic radiation loop through the temporal lobe (Meyer’s loop); damage there causes a contralateral upper quadrant field loss.
Fibres for the pupillary light reflex leave the optic tract for the pretectal area.

topics.title: Auditory and Vestibular Pathways
topics.summary: The pathways of hearing and balance.
points: Hearing: cochlear hair cells, cochlear nerve, cochlear nuclei, superior olivary complex, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate body and primary auditory cortex in the superior temporal gyrus.
Each ear is represented in both hemispheres, so damage to one auditory cortex does not cause deafness in one ear.

Balance: the semicircular canals sense rotation and the utricle and saccule sense linear movement and gravity; their signals go to the vestibular nuclei and on to the eye muscles, spinal cord and cerebellum.
The Rinne and Weber tests distinguish conductive from sensorineural hearing loss.

topics.title: Plain Radiography
topics.summary: X-ray images made by passing X-rays through the body onto a detector.
points: Dense tissues absorb more X-rays, so they appear whiter.
Five basic densities are seen: air (black), fat, soft tissue and fluid, bone, and metal (white).
A posteroanterior chest radiograph is preferred because it does not magnify the heart.
The dose is low, but X-rays are ionising radiation.

topics.title: Computed Tomography
topics.summary: Cross-sectional X-ray imaging reconstructed by computer (CT).
points: An X-ray tube rotates around the patient and a computer builds slices from the measurements.
Density is measured in Hounsfield units: water 0, air −1000 and dense bone about +1000.
It is fast and is the first-line scan in major trauma and in stroke, to exclude bleeding.
Its radiation dose is higher than that of plain radiographs; iodinated contrast shows vessels and organs.

topics.title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging
topics.summary: Imaging with a strong magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses (MRI).
points: It uses no ionising radiation.
On T1-weighted images fat is bright and fluid dark; on T2-weighted images fluid is bright.
It is the best method for soft tissue: brain, spinal cord, joints and pelvis.
Some implants and metal foreign bodies make it unsafe, so every patient is screened first.

topics.title: Ultrasonography
topics.summary: Real-time imaging with high-frequency sound waves.
points: It uses no radiation and is portable and repeatable.
It is good for soft tissues and fluid: the pregnant uterus, the heart (echocardiography), vessels and abdominal organs.
Air and bone block the sound, limiting views of the lungs and of structures behind bowel gas or bone.
Its quality depends on the skill of the operator.

topics.title: Angiography
topics.summary: Imaging of blood vessels with contrast.
points: It can be done by catheter (digital subtraction angiography), CT or MRI.
Digital subtraction removes the background of bone and soft tissue to show only the vessels.
Coronary angiography diagnoses coronary artery disease and guides its treatment with stents.
It shows narrowings, blockages, aneurysms and sites of bleeding.

topics.title: Cross-Sectional Imaging
topics.summary: Imaging that shows the body in slices: CT, MRI and ultrasound.
points: Axial slices are viewed as if from the patient’s feet, so the patient’s right appears on the viewer’s left.
CT window settings change the grey scale to show lung, soft tissue or bone.
Thin slices can be rebuilt in other planes or as 3D images.
Comparing slices with known anatomy at standard levels makes scans easier to read.
